STMPA.PA.happening: STMicroelectronics is breaking out as European auto-semi pricing inflects and the company's silicon-carbide (SiC) MOSFET wafer ramp at Catania crosses commercial scale. After two cyclical years of weak auto and industrial demand, lead times have shortened and channel inventory is cleared.
STMPA.PA.why: Three tailwinds align: (1) Chinese EV OEMs are locking multi-year SiC supply deals with non-Wolfspeed sources, putting STM in front of every major Tier-1; (2) Apple silicon and microcontroller wins are starting to flow through into 2026 revenue guidance; (3) the firm's net cash position lets it run buybacks while peers (Infineon, NXP) are deleveraging. STM trades at a P/E discount to US semis despite SiC leadership.
STMPA.PA.risk: Watch: SiC pricing competition from Chinese substrate suppliers (TankeBlue, SICC) is real and could compress margins if it shows up in 1H26 guidance. Also, any pause in EV OEM SiC adoption — Tesla is still wavering between SiC and IGBT in lower-trim trucks. Suggested stop ≈ 2× ATR below; reduce size if hyperscaler capex commentary turns cautious into next earnings.
STMPA.PA.business: Franco-Italian semiconductor maker. Makes microcontrollers, analog/power chips, and silicon-carbide (SiC) power transistors. Big in automotive (EV/ADAS), industrial automation, and IoT — supplies almost every European car maker and is Apple's secure-element vendor.

thesis.statement: STMicroelectronics is breaking out as European auto-semi pricing inflects and the company's silicon-carbide (SiC) MOSFET wafer ramp at Catania crosses commercial scale.

SNDK.happening: Sandisk's post-spinoff identity as a pure-play NAND/SSD operator is paying off as enterprise SSD pricing rises sharply and HDD-to-SSD substitution accelerates in data centers. Pricing power has returned faster than the sell-side modeled — both contract and spot prices on enterprise QLC are at multi-quarter highs.
SNDK.why: AI-training workloads need cheap, fast, high-density storage for checkpoint data and inference caching — exactly Sandisk's BiCS8 sweet spot. Three of the four US hyperscalers have publicly increased NAND allocations for 2026. Industry NAND capex remains restrained (Samsung and Hynix are prioritizing HBM), keeping supply tight through 2026.
SNDK.risk: Watch: NAND is the most cyclical memory segment. A single hyperscaler pause (which is rare but has happened before) can rapidly push contract pricing back down. Also, Sandisk's balance sheet is thinner than peers — any working-capital squeeze in a downturn is more painful. Earnings volatility is structural.
SNDK.business: Pure-play NAND flash memory + SSD manufacturer, spun out of Western Digital in 2025. Makes the storage chips that go inside enterprise data-center SSDs, consumer SSDs, and memory cards.

DOCN.why: DOCN's pricing model (transparent flat-rate vs hyperscaler complexity) is finally a meaningful differentiator now that AI workloads have become mainstream for indie devs and SMB SaaS. Recent product launches (managed inference, vector DB) close the gap with AWS for sub-100-employee customers. Insider buying in the last quarter was notable.
DOCN.risk: Watch: DOCN is a $4B market-cap business competing against trillion-dollar hyperscalers. Any meaningful AWS/GCP price drop on small-instance compute hurts the moat. Also, GPU droplet revenue concentration in a handful of generative-AI startups creates customer-concentration risk that doesn't show in headline numbers.
DOCN.business: Cloud computing platform aimed at developers and small/medium businesses. Think of it as the affordable, simple alternative to AWS — flat-rate virtual servers ('droplets'), managed databases, and GPU compute, popular with indie developers and startups.

NOD.OL.happening: Nordic Semiconductor is breaking out on a clear inflection in Bluetooth Low Energy + Wi-Fi 6 chip demand for wearables, hearables, and smart-home, plus first revenue from cellular IoT (nRF91 series). After a two-year inventory correction, the channel is finally rebuilding.
NOD.OL.why: Three converging catalysts: (1) Apple Vision Pro 2 and Meta Ray-Ban supply wins are starting to ship in volume; (2) the cellular IoT category (asset tracking, smart meters) is moving from pilot to deployment; (3) Nordic remains the only Western vendor with credible scale in low-power Bluetooth — geopolitical preference is real here. NOD.OL.risk: Watch: Wearables demand is consumer-cyclical and tied to Apple/Meta product cycles — a weak holiday quarter can quickly reverse. Also, Chinese competition in low-end BLE (Telink, Bouffalo) compresses ASPs at the entry tier. Position sizing should reflect single-customer concentration risk.
NOD.OL.business: Norwegian semiconductor company specializing in low-power wireless chips. Makes the Bluetooth Low Energy chips inside most wearables, hearables (AirPods, Galaxy Buds), smart-home devices, and increasingly cellular-IoT devices like asset trackers and smart meters.

TSMC's ramp at Phoenix and the broader CoWoS expansion are unlocking the order book the market had partly written off.
BESI.AS.why: BESI's hybrid-bonding monopoly is the closest thing to ASML's EUV lock-in within back-end semis. BESI.AS.business: Dutch semiconductor equipment company. Makes back-end packaging machinery — specifically hybrid bonding tools that stack chips on top of each other (required for HBM memory and advanced AI accelerators). Near-monopoly position alongside Applied Materials in this niche.

STX.why: AI workloads create more cold/warm data than they consume hot — every training run produces enormous archived datasets that economically belong on HDD. STX.risk: Watch: any major QLC NAND pricing collapse could re-open the HDD-substitution conversation, especially in mid-tier nearline. Also, STX's customer concentration is among the highest in semis (top 3 = >50% of revenue) — single-customer renegotiation risk is real.
STX.business: Hard disk drive (HDD) manufacturer. Makes the spinning-disk storage used in data centers for 'nearline' (warm/cold) storage of huge datasets — exactly what AI training generates as archived data.

PBF.happening: PBF is breaking out on a refining-margin windfall: Q2 adjusted EPS of $6.22 crushed the $3.49 estimate as geopolitically-tightened product markets lifted cracks, and management slashed net debt by over $1.4B (net-debt/capital 36% -> 15%) while signaling elevated margins could persist into 2027. W.business: Pure-play online retailer of furniture and home goods (Wayfair.com, AllModern, Birch Lane, Joss & Main, Perigold, Wayfair Professional). It carries little inventory — ~20,000 third-party suppliers list and ship bulky items through Wayfair's CastleGate warehouses and last-mile network, with Wayfair taking a retail margin. The moat is vertical logistics scale in damage-prone bulky home delivery; customer switching costs are near zero.
W.happening: W is breaking out on its best US revenue growth of the post-COVID era: Q2 (4 Aug) net revenue +7.5% with orders +6% and a 6.9% adjusted EBITDA margin (highest since 2021), sending shares up ~19%. Suggested stop ~2x ATR below; W is high-beta and macro-levered — size accordingly and trim on weak housing data.

UNI.MI.business: Italy's leading non-life insurer (especially motor and health) and a major life insurer, following the 2024 merger that absorbed UnipolSai into the holding. It sells through the largest tied-agent network in Italy plus bancassurance via its ~20% stake in bank BPER. FY2025 total premiums rose 11.1% to EUR 17.4B, net profit rose ~40% to EUR 1.2B, the non-life combined ratio was 91.0% and solvency 218%. The moat is distribution scale plus the country's biggest motor-telematics book, giving a proprietary pricing/claims-data edge, though it's concentrated in Italy.
UNI.MI.happening: UNI is grinding higher on a steady beat-and-deliver story: Q1 (15 May) was in line (EPS EUR 0.51, net profit ~EUR 329m +15%) with the combined ratio hitting the 90% industrial-plan KPI level, and management raised the cumulative 2025-27 dividend target to >=EUR 2.4bn and set 'more than EUR 800m' as an annual distribution floor. Insurance-group solvency ~300% underpins the capital-return story. This is a defensive, high-yield compounder re-rating on plan delivery and rising cash distributions.
UNI.MI.why: Three tailwinds: (1) best-in-class underwriting — the combined ratio reached the 90% plan-level KPI with deliberately extra-prudent reserving (attritional loss ratio nudged to ~69% with 'no adverse claims trend'), seeding future prior-year releases; motor is growing (retail MTPL pricing ~+3% plus the Stellantis distribution deal); (2) bancassurance momentum — premiums grew >30% with the Banca Popolare di Sondrio integration and agents channel +20%; (3) fortress capital — a EUR 1bn Restricted Tier 1 plus organic generation put insurance-group solvency ~300%, funding a raised >=EUR 2.4bn cumulative dividend and a >EUR 800m annual floor. Trades at a low P/E with a high, cash-only dividend yield; the valuation angle is durable capital return from a market-leading Italian franchise.
UNI.MI.risk: Watch: (1) single-market concentration — results are tied to Italian GDP, motor frequency/severity and BTP sovereign-spread moves on the investment portfolio (investment income was ~EUR 50m below Q1'25 on soft markets); (2) motor-pricing cyclicality and claims inflation (repair costs, bodily injury) could erode the strong combined ratio if premium hardening reverses; (3) the bancassurance strategy depends on the BPER relationship and BPER's own M&A (Banca Popolare di Sondrio offer), and management is buyback-averse (cash-dividend-only), capping return flexibility. Suggested stop ~2x ATR below; this is a low-beta income name — trim on a combined-ratio deterioration or a sharp BTP-spread widening.

ACHC.why: Three tailwinds align: (1) the cash-flow inflection — capex cut to $235-255m with operating cash flow guided up to $350-400m, as the 2023-26 bed-building cohort turns from cash drag into ~$200m of incremental EBITDA once startup losses peak in Q3 and roll off; (2) Osteen's reset is showing where it matters — residential treatment +12%, 300+ beds added in H1 toward 500-600 for 2026, net leverage down to ~4.1x; (3) valuation is at crisis levels — a mid-single-digit EV/EBITDA and single-digit P/E on $1.45-1.60 guided EPS price in permanent Medicaid impairment, so any policy calm or clean quarter re-rates it.
ACHC.risk: Watch the DOJ investigations (SDNY, W.D. Missouri) into admissions and billing — headline risk can gap the stock regardless of fundamentals — and the $28.6m prior-year liability true-up shows reserve risk is still live. Suggested stop ≈ 2× ATR below; keep size modest — this is a show-me turnaround with legal tail risk.

BBY.business: The last national US consumer-electronics big-box chain (~1,100 stores, $41.7bn revenue) — the physical showroom Apple, Samsung and HP need now that Circuit City and hhgregg are gone. Thin-margin product retail is increasingly subsidized by the high-margin attach layer: Geek Squad services, paid memberships, the Best Buy Ads retail-media arm and a third-party marketplace.
BBY.happening: Momentum stems from a Q1 FY27 beat (May 28: comps +2%, adjusted EPS +11%) that management deliberately did not flow through to guidance — the implied Q2 deceleration is Switch 2 and Windows-10 lap math, not demand rollover, with May comps running high-single-digit. Add a well-received CEO succession (27-year veteran Jason Bonfig from Nov 1) pitching Best Buy as a 'retailer, media, advertising and technology company', plus an AI-PC refresh cycle powering the ninth straight positive computing comp, and the set-up into the late-August print is a beat against a sandbagged bar.
BBY.why: Three tailwinds align: (1) a structural margin-mix shift — Marketplace GMV scaling toward a >=$1.2bn FY27 target and Best Buy Ads toward ~$1bn of collections are both gross-margin accretive (+20bps already), slowly de-commoditizing the P&L; (2) the computing cycle has legs — AI PCs and the Windows 10 end-of-life refresh, with inventory deliberately pre-bought ahead of memory-driven cost increases and a ~1-year RGB TV exclusive layering on; (3) valuation and carry — roughly 11-12x guided EPS ($6.30-6.60) with a ~4% dividend yield, and guidance held flat despite the Q1 beat leaves room for raises through the year.
BBY.risk: Watch tariffs and DRAM-driven hardware cost inflation — Best Buy holds pricing power only while vendors fund it, and demand destruction from price hikes is the FY27 wildcard; comps guidance of -1% to +1% means the bull case leans heavily on the AI-PC cycle materializing. Vendor concentration (five suppliers = ~55% of purchases) and the structural Amazon/Walmart price war cap product margins. Suggested stop ≈ 2× ATR below; the Q2 print in late August is the near-term make-or-break.

TOST.business: The cloud operating system for restaurants: POS hardware sold near cost, SaaS modules (online ordering, payroll, kitchen display, AI) and embedded payments across ~180,000 locations — about 16% of US restaurant payment volume. Ripping Toast out means retraining staff and rewiring money flows, and its data density feeds AI products (Toast IQ) that no single-vertical rival can match.
TOST.happening: Q2 (Aug 4) was a beat-and-raise with a narrative upgrade: record 9,500 net location adds (1,000 above the prior high watermark), recurring gross profit +28%, adjusted EBITDA of $221m at a 37% margin smashing the guide, and a second straight FY26 guidance hike. Management simultaneously repositioned Toast as an agentic-AI company — Toast IQ Grow is the fastest product in company history to $10m ARR — giving the stock a fundamentals beat and an AI story in the same print.
TOST.why: Three tailwinds align: (1) the land engine keeps accelerating into new TAMs — enterprise (Best Western endorsement, Kung Fu Tea), international (TGI Fridays UK) and food retail/gas stations, with new-market ARR on track to nearly double to $200m in 2026; (2) AI is a genuine ARPU lever, not vapor — IQ Grow case studies show 70% marketing-cost cuts and $100k+ of attributed sales, with voice, payroll, inventory and bookkeeping agents queued behind it en route to a $10bn ARR ambition; (3) profitability is inflecting fast — recurring gross profit guided to 23-25% growth, EBITDA guide raised again, 40%+ long-term margin target reiterated. The valuation angle: a rich growth multiple, so estimate momentum, not cheapness, is doing the lifting.
TOST.risk: Watch the 2027 DRAM/memory hardware-cost headwind — the CFO confirmed it hits the 2027 P&L harder than 2026 via inventory accounting, making the FY27 guide (Feb 2027) the key risk event. GPV per location has been soft (~-1% y/y in Q1), so a consumer dining pullback flows straight through the fintech take rate, and Toast Capital credit losses would spike in a restaurant-closure wave. Suggested stop ≈ 2× ATR below; tighten into the Q3 print if the stock runs further ahead of estimates.

VLO.business: Valero buys crude and other feedstocks, runs them through 15 refineries in the US, Canada and the UK totalling ~3.2m bpd, and sells gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and petrochemical feedstocks wholesale and through ~7,000 branded outlets. Roughly 60% of throughput sits on the US Gulf Coast on deep-water docks, which lets it buy discounted waterborne sour and heavy crude and export product into Latin America and Europe when domestic cracks soften. Two smaller legs sit alongside: Diamond Green Diesel, the 50/50 renewable diesel and SAF JV with Darling Ingredients (~1.2bn gal/yr), and 12 Mid-Continent ethanol plants (~1.7bn gal/yr). It earns a spread, not a price — crack margin times throughput is the entire model.
VLO.happening: Q2 2026 was a blowout: net income of $3.7bn ($12.62/share, adjusted $12.54 versus $10.03 consensus) on $44.5bn of revenue, with refining operating income of $4.5bn against $1.3bn a year ago. Diamond Green Diesel swung to $717M of operating income from a $79M loss, an ~$800M year-over-year turn. Valero returned $2.6bn in the quarter at a 59% payout ratio and declared a $1.20 quarterly dividend.
VLO.why: Three things are driving it. (1) Low global product inventories and limited spare refining capacity are setting cracks, and management is explicitly arguing the mid-cycle floor is now anchored by Northwest European hydroskimming economics rather than historical cracking margins — that is a request to re-rate through-cycle earnings power, not just the 2026 print. (2) Renewable diesel flipped from drag to profit engine on favourable RIN values and a supportive RVO, removing the single loudest bear talking point of 2025. (3) Portfolio pruning is real — refining operations ceased at Benicia, California (~$33M of incremental depreciation recognised), taking out a structurally disadvantaged West Coast asset exposed to CARB and LCFS. Capital investment stays at ~$2.0bn attributable to Valero, ~$1.7bn of it sustaining, so incremental cash goes straight to buybacks and the dividend. On valuation, refiners are capitalised on mid-cycle EPS rather than the trailing print, so annualising a $12.54 quarter leaves VLO on a very low trailing multiple alongside Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 — the re-rating case is entirely whether the hydroskimming-floor argument moves the mid-cycle number the market actually uses.
VLO.risk: Watch: management is deliberately holding cash above its own $4-5bn long-term target as a working-capital hedge, with CFO Homer Bhullar framing the risk as 'a rapid pullback in commodity prices, particularly crude' — which reads as management not trusting the durability of this cycle even while printing records. Renewable diesel's swing was policy-driven (RIN values, RVO), so a change in the 45Z credit regime or feedstock tariffs reverses $700M+ of operating income quickly, and Neste remains the global cost leader able to pressure DGD's spread independent of policy. The West Coast residual and California's refining-margin penalty legislation are a live regulatory tail. Suggested stop ≈ 2× ATR below entry; size this as a cyclical rather than a compounder and cut on the first sequentially negative crack spread commentary.

CRDO.business: Credo sells the high-speed interconnect that links servers and GPUs inside AI datacentres. Its signature product is the ZeroFlap Active Electrical Cable — a copper cable with Credo's own SerDes silicon in the connector — which replaces short-reach optics at lower power and cost with far better link reliability. It also sells optical DSPs, ZeroFlap optical transceivers, OmniConnect memory connectivity, PCIe/Ethernet retimers and SerDes chiplets, and licenses its SerDes IP. Buyers are hyperscalers, neocloud operators, ODMs and optical module makers; the top ten customers were roughly 90% of FY2026 revenue.
CRDO.happening: FY2026 (ended May 2026) revenue tripled to $1.335bn, up 206% year over year, with Q4 a record $437M (+157%) above the high end of guidance. On the 1 June call Credo raised FY27 growth framing from 'greater than 50%' to 'greater than 80%', with the optical portfolio alone guided above $600M. Q1 FY27 is guided to $465-475M at a 67-69% non-GAAP gross margin.
CRDO.why: The mechanism has three parts. (1) The story converted from an AEC pure-play into an AEC-plus-optical franchise: optical DSPs, silicon photonics PICs and ZeroFlap optics are each expected to clear $100M in FY27 with acceleration weighted to 2H, and the Dust Photonics acquisition closed the week before the call adding a silicon photonics platform (the ~$750M net cash outflow lands in Q1 FY27). (2) Management guided FY27 gross margin 'broadly consistent' with FY26's 68.1% despite a heavier optical mix — a direct rebuttal of the core bear case that optical is structurally dilutive to AEC-level margins. (3) The customer base is broadening past the original two hyperscalers, with CEO Bill Brennan calling out neoclouds, sovereign AI, enterprise and inference/agentic workloads as the incremental vector, and Customer A falling from 66% to 53% of revenue. Underneath all of it is the 'n-1' advantage: Credo's mixed-signal SerDes architecture hits competitive performance on an older, cheaper, more available process node, so it prices under Broadcom and Marvell while still earning 68% gross margins without queuing for leading-edge TSMC capacity. Valuation is the hard part — CRDO carries a steep premium to Broadcom, Marvell and Astera Labs on every revenue and earnings multiple, and the >80% FY27 guide at 68% gross margin is the entire justification.
CRDO.risk: Watch: supply, not demand, is the governor on the FY27 guide — Brennan conceded tightness persists on the ZeroFlap optics ramp, so a partner miss compresses the number with no change in demand at all. Two customers were each above 10% of FY26 revenue with no long-term purchase commitments, making the order book effectively at-will, and wafers are sole-sourced at TSMC through a small set of Asian OSATs and cable manufacturers. Copper AECs also carry a physics ceiling — as lane rates move to 200G and 400G per lane the reach shortens and the addressable copper socket can migrate to optics faster than Credo's optical leg scales, while Broadcom, Marvell and Astera Labs (whose Scorpio fabric switch just became its largest product family at $392.4M of Q2 revenue) all attack the same rack-scale interconnect budget. Size small and use a wide stop — a single hyperscaler capex pause resets the model, and this name gaps.

HALO.business: Halozyme is a royalty machine, not a drug company. Its enzyme rHuPH20 temporarily breaks down hyaluronan under the skin so large-volume biologics can be injected subcutaneously in minutes instead of infused for hours. It licenses that technology as ENHANZE to big pharma — Janssen, Roche, argenx, Bristol Myers Squibb, Takeda — which reformulates blockbusters as subcutaneous versions and pays royalties on the resulting sales; ten ENHANZE products are commercial in 100+ markets. It also sells proprietary products (Hylenex, XYOSTED), supplies bulk rHuPH20 API, and has bought two hyperconcentration platforms, Hypercon from Elektrofi and Surf Bio.
HALO.happening: Q2 2026, reported 6 August, was a record and a big raise — revenue up 48% year over year to $481M against roughly $402M consensus, royalties up 50% to $307.7M and adjusted EBITDA up 46% to $328.8M. FY26 guidance was lifted $112.5M at the midpoint to $1.835-1.91bn with royalties guided to $1.22-1.245bn (41-43% growth). A new $1bn buyback authorisation was announced on top of the $332.8M already repurchased in Q2.
HALO.why: Four things are compounding. (1) The royalty base has broadened well beyond DARZALEX SC and VYVGART Hytrulo — OCREVUS ZUNOVO, Opdivo Qvantig and RYBREVANT SC are now contributing materially, which directly attacks the single-product-concentration bear case. (2) Five new collaboration agreements signed year to date generated $35.5M of upfront revenue, which CEO Helen Torley called the strongest pace of new collaborations in company history, and the Hypercon and Surf Bio deals extend platform economics into the 2040s — when pressed on the durability of the raise, Torley leaned on duration rather than 2026 launch timing. (3) The guidance carries zero Keytruda royalty: Halozyme holds a Munich Regional Court preliminary injunction from December 2025 blocking Merck's subcutaneous Keytruda in Germany on EP 2797622, while MSD invalidated one US MDASE patent at the PTAB in May 2026 — so US pembrolizumab economics are pure option value and the $112.5M raise stands entirely without them. On valuation, guided FY26 non-GAAP diluted EPS of $8.65-9.00 puts HALO at a strikingly low forward P/E for a business compounding royalties at 41-43%; the market is pricing the rHuPH20 patent cliff, not the compounding.
HALO.risk: Watch: the core rHuPH20 estate faces a patent cliff around 2027, and the entire valuation rests on whether coformulation and MDASE claims plus contract terms carry royalties into the 2030s. Alteogen's ALT-B4, licensed to Merck, proves a workaround exists — the German injunction is a jurisdiction-limited defence and IP litigation alone cost $16.7M in 2025. Concentration is still real underneath the diversification narrative: Janssen's DARZALEX FASPRO remains the single largest royalty stream, so a biosimilar entry or formulary shift there hits harder than the headline suggests. Position modestly given binary legal outcomes, and treat an adverse PTAB or Federal Circuit ruling on the MDASE estate as a thesis-ender to exit rather than a drawdown to average into.

MPC.business: Marathon Petroleum runs the largest refining system in the United States — 2,986 mbpcd of crude capacity across 13 refineries on the Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent and West Coast — and sells the output wholesale and through roughly 7,000 Marathon- and ARCO-branded outlets, including a 15-year, ~7.7bn gallon per year supply agreement with 7-Eleven. Bolted onto it is MPLX, a publicly traded midstream partnership MPC controls through the general partner and ~64% of the units, which gathers, processes and transports crude, natural gas, NGLs and refined products on fee-based contracts. A much smaller renewable diesel segment (Dickinson, North Dakota and the Martinez, California JV with Neste) rounds it out and remains loss-making. The structure is what differentiates it: MPLX converts cyclical refining into a semi-contracted cash annuity.
MPC.happening: Q2 2026, reported 4 August, was a record refining quarter — adjusted EBITDA of $8.5bn and EPS of $17.73 against $14.52 consensus, on a 112% R&M margin capture. The capture came from crude optimisation rather than headline cracks: advantaged SPR barrels plus heavier Canadian and Venezuelan crude in the slate. MPC returned $2.8bn in the quarter, $2.5bn of it buybacks.
MPC.why: The mechanism has three legs. (1) The 112% capture is a slate-and-logistics result, not a pure crack result — MPC monetised cheap SPR and heavy sour barrels that its Gulf Coast and Mid-Continent complexity can process, which is precisely the edge scale is supposed to buy. (2) MPLX is the funded growth engine: 2026 growth capex was raised $500M to $2.9bn on accelerated Gulf Coast fractionation work, underwriting 12.5% annual distribution growth in both 2026 and 2027 and rising cash distributions back to the parent, where the midstream distribution alone more than covers MPC's dividend. (3) Capital return discipline is the third leg — $7.8bn of cash sits against a stated operating cash target of roughly $1bn, and CEO Maryann Mannen told Goldman Sachs and Wolfe Research that buybacks remain the preferred vehicle, framing the balance as a timing artefact and pointing to sustained elevated repurchases rather than a special distribution. Versus Valero, MPC is the more midstream-insulated way to own the same crack cycle; both are capitalised on mid-cycle EPS well below the trailing print, with FY25 adjusted EPS of $10.70 the number the market anchors to rather than $17.73 annualised.
MPC.risk: Watch: management pre-warned that roughly $290M of Q3 turnaround expense concentrated in Gulf Coast and MidCon conversion units will limit product upgrading, explicitly flagging Q2's 112% capture as a high-water mark, with Q3 throughput guided to ~2.8m bpd at 94% utilisation. Renewable diesel lost $110M of segment adjusted EBITDA in 2025 and the 45Z credit transition plus feedstock tariffs remain unresolved. California regulatory risk on West Coast assets — windfall-profit taxes and maximum-refining-margin penalties — is a live tail, and the SPR-barrel advantage is by definition finite. Treat this as a cycle trade rather than a hold: stop ≈ 2× ATR below entry and reduce on any sequential capture deterioration in the Q3 print.

PAYC.business: Paycom sells one cloud HCM system to US mid-market employers — payroll, tax filing, time and attendance, hiring, benefits and expense management all writing to a single database with one employee record, so there is no HRIS-to-payroll integration layer to break. It charges recurring per-employee-per-month fees and keeps the interest on payroll funds held between the employer debit and payday. The base is roughly 39,200 clients and 7.4m employee records, sold direct through about 55 US sales offices, concentrated in the 50-10,000 employee band with a sweet spot at 100-2,500. Core verticals are healthcare and senior care, restaurants and hospitality, retail, manufacturing and logistics — high-turnover hourly workforces where payroll complexity is the pain.
PAYC.happening: Q2 2026, reported 5 August, was a beat-and-raise — revenue of $531.2M (+9.8% year over year), non-GAAP EPS of $2.78 (16.8% above consensus) and adjusted EBITDA of $235M at a 44.2% margin. FY26 revenue guidance moved to $2.197-2.212bn from $2.175-2.195bn. The stock rose roughly 14% pre-market and BTIG lifted its price target from $160 to $230.
PAYC.why: Three drivers. (1) Automation is finally showing up as operating leverage rather than a talking point — CEO Chad Richison tied the beat directly to Beti (employee-driven payroll) and the IWant AI engine, which gives instant natural-language access to employee data without navigating the software, and the full-year guide implies roughly 46% adjusted EBITDA margin against the 44.2% delivered in Q2. (2) The setup is a classic guidance-conservatism re-rate: Q2 grew 9.8% while the full-year guide implies only ~7-8%, so management raised while deliberately keeping the second-half bar below the run rate, which is precisely why the stock gapped on the print. (3) Recurring revenue growth of 8-9% runs ahead of total reported growth because the float headwind is now explicit and quantified — interest on client funds fell to $26.0M from $28.5M with ~$105M expected for the year — meaning the underlying subscription business is healthier than the headline. On valuation, roughly $1.0bn of FY26 adjusted EBITDA against a share count near 56m leaves PAYC in the low-double-digit EV/EBITDA range, a material discount to ADP and Paylocity for a business running mid-40s margins.
PAYC.risk: Watch: float income is close to 100% incremental margin, so a Fed cutting cycle hits EPS harder than it hits revenue — the ~$105M 2026 figure is the line to track quarter by quarter. Paychex's April 2025 acquisition of Paycor put a far better-funded rival directly into Paycom's mid-market band, alongside Paylocity head-to-head in the 50-5,000 seat range and ADP as the incumbent Paycom must displace to grow. Management framed IWant and Beti as retention and cost-to-serve levers rather than incremental per-seat pricing, which means the AI story is defensive economics first and monetisation only later — do not underwrite it as a growth reacceleration. Size to a 7-8% grower rather than a 20% one, and use the ~46% full-year margin guide as the falsification checkpoint.

ATI.business: ATI melts, forges, rolls and machines specialty metals — titanium, nickel-based superalloys, zirconium, hafnium and specialty stainless — into the mill products and precision components that go into jet engines and airframes. It is one of only a handful of Western producers qualified to supply rotating-grade material for commercial jet engines, and sells largely under multi-year long-term agreements rather than on spot. Two segments: High Performance Materials & Components (titanium and nickel forgings, castings and powders) and Advanced Alloys & Solutions (titanium, nickel and specialty stainless plate, sheet, strip and precision rolled). Customers are GE Aerospace, Safran, Rolls-Royce, Pratt & Whitney, Boeing, Airbus, Howmet and the US naval nuclear programme.
ATI.happening: Q2 2026, reported 6 August, delivered the strongest quarterly EBITDA since 2007 — $284m, up 37%, on $1.3bn of revenue with margin up 440bps to 22.6%. Management raised the FY26 adjusted EBITDA midpoint to $1.16bn (+35% year over year) and reframed AA&S from a cyclical stainless business into a structurally mid-20s-margin aerospace and defence franchise. Backlog hit a record $4.4bn, and Howmet's same-day 24% revenue growth confirmed the whole specialty-materials layer is inflecting together.
ATI.why: Three drivers. (1) AA&S has been genuinely de-cyclicalised — aerospace and defence is now 44% of segment revenue, more than double its share five years ago, after ATI exited standard stainless, and ATI is one of only three qualified Western producers of high-purity hafnium and zirconium exactly as China restricts exports into aerospace and nuclear markets. (2) Defence revenue hit an all-time high, up 36% year over year on naval nuclear, missile and missile-defence demand, with a renewed naval nuclear contract running through 2030 that more than doubles annual revenue versus the prior agreement on improved pricing and mix; jet engine revenue rose 13% with content on next-generation platforms more than double legacy. (3) Capacity, not demand, is the binding constraint — premium-quality titanium lead times have extended to 20 months and isothermal forgings sit above 24 months, which is why consolidated incremental margins were guided up from ~40% to ~50%, Q3 EBITDA to $305-315m and Q4 to the strongest quarter of the year at an implied ~$1.35bn annualised exit rate. Against an FY26 adjusted EPS midpoint of $5.04 (+56% year over year) and ~$575m of free cash flow, ATI still trades at a discount to Howmet and Carpenter Technology on forward earnings — the re-rating case is that the market is still pricing a stainless cyclical rather than an aero-defence franchise.
ATI.risk: Watch: the second-half hockey stick is qualification-gated — roughly $30-40m of HPMC revenue shifted from H1 to H2 on qualification timing at the new Mexico facility and the EB2 furnace, and those shipments carry 40-50% incremental margins, so the ~$1.35bn Q4 exit rate underpinning 2027 expectations is the number at risk if quals slip again. Free cash flow did not rise with the EBITDA raise; management attributed the gap to receivables timing and inventory build for early 2027, which pushes the cash proof of the margin reset into next year. Programme concentration is real — commercial jet engines alone are ~39% of sales, so a Boeing 737 MAX or Airbus A320neo rate cut flows straight through, while Precision Castparts, Howmet and Carpenter Technology compete for the same qualified sockets. Use a wide stop given the beta to OEM build rates, and treat a second qualification delay at Mexico or EB2 as the signal to cut rather than average down.

PATH.business: UiPath sells enterprise automation software. Its original product is RPA — software robots that drive existing applications through their user interfaces to run rules-based back-office work like invoice matching, claims intake and ERP data entry, with no integration project required. It now sells the same platform as agentic automation: deterministic robots plus LLM-based agents, governed centrally through Orchestrator, with Maestro handling cross-system process orchestration. Largest verticals are banking and financial services, insurance, healthcare and US federal (FedRAMP-authorised Automation Cloud), sold both direct and through Accenture, Deloitte, EY and BPO partners who embed UiPath in their own delivery.
PATH.happening: Q1 FY2027, reported 28 May 2026, was UiPath's first GAAP-profitable quarter in company history — $28m of GAAP operating income on revenue up 17% to $418m. Non-GAAP operating income was $92m at a 22% margin, with $130m of adjusted free cash flow, $1.4bn of cash and no debt. FY27 revenue guidance was raised to $1.776-1.781bn despite an incremental FX headwind.
PATH.why: Three things. (1) The profitability inflection is real and the underlying metrics are clean — 83% total and 90% software gross margin, 97% gross retention, RPO up 15% to $1.413bn and $1m+ ARR customers up 18% to 374, so the enterprise base is where the growth actually sits. (2) AI has become the deal driver rather than an add-on: 16 of the top 20 deals in the quarter included AI components and expansion deals with AI attached were roughly six times larger than those without, with Maestro acting as the wedge for larger landings in complex orchestration spanning humans, task automation, enterprise workflows and agents. (3) Valuation is doing most of the work — net of $1.4bn of cash and no debt, enterprise value sits at a low-single-digit multiple of the $2.058-2.063bn FY27 ARR guide, so the market has priced PATH as a melting RPA asset and any evidence that agentic automation re-accelerates ARR re-rates the multiple rather than just the estimates. The honest counterweight is that ARR grew only 12% to $1.901bn on $49m of net new ARR, so this is a valuation-plus-inflection setup, not a growth story.
PATH.risk: Watch: Microsoft Power Automate is bundled into M365 E5, which removes the budget line for entry-level RPA outright — dollar-based net retention has slid from 118% in Q1 FY2025 to 109% in Q1 FY2027, and that trend line is the thesis. Management described the demand environment as 'stable' rather than improving, which is the tell: growth is coming from AI attach on large deals, not a broad recovery. On competition, management defended on integration breadth and legacy reach rather than model quality — an implicit concession that it will not compete at the model layer against ServiceNow, Salesforce Agentforce or the LLM labs' own computer-use frameworks, while Automation Anywhere and SS&C Blue Prism fight for the same install base and US federal procurement pauses bite a meaningful vertical. Keep the position small, anchor to the Q2 FY27 ARR guide of $1.929-1.934bn, and exit if net new ARR fails to inflect above the $49m run rate.

U.business: Unity runs two businesses. Create Solutions licenses the Unity game engine — the development environment behind roughly 70% of the top mobile games — on per-seat Pro and Enterprise subscriptions plus cloud and hosting, extending into Unity Industry for automotive HMI, AEC visualisation and defence simulation. Grow Solutions is the larger and more important half: a mobile ad network (Unity Ads and ironSource) with LevelPlay mediation, monetised as a share of advertiser spend and now powered by the Unity Vector AI ranking engine. Its customers are simultaneously its supply and its demand — mobile studios build on the engine, sell the ad inventory and buy the user acquisition. FY2025 revenue was $1.85bn, roughly two-thirds Grow and one-third Create.
U.happening: Q2 2026, reported 6 August, was in CEO Matt Bromberg's words 'arguably the best quarter in Unity's history as a public company'. Vector grew 23% sequentially against 12-13% guidance and crossed a $1bn annualised run rate two quarters early, adjusted EBITDA margin hit a record 29%, and GAAP profitability was pulled forward to Q3, two quarters ahead of the prior target. Q3 strategic revenue is guided to $540-550m (+44-47% year over year) with Grow Solutions up 68-70%.
U.why: Three mechanisms. (1) The moat argument finally has evidence: late in Q2, Unity for the first time fed first-party runtime signals from roughly 3 billion monthly players into Vector's prediction models — Bromberg called it 'very early' but the results 'extremely encouraging' — and CFO Jarrod Yahes confirmed the ironSource ad network shutdown contributed only $3m, so the 23% sequential gain was organic rather than migration. (2) Product velocity is compounding: Day 28 ROAS extended the measurement window beyond the standard seven days, more than 25% of the advertiser base adopted it and spend on those campaigns nearly tripled sequentially, one of over 20 major product updates shipped in the quarter. (3) The margin expansion is funded by not spending — Bromberg told Bank of America's Omar Dessouky that in gaming 'the vast majority of folks already know who we are', so growth comes from optimising and scaling existing clients rather than prospecting, which is precisely how Q3 EBITDA of $185-190m at a ~33% margin (roughly 1,000bps of year-over-year expansion) gets paid for. Create is being re-platformed alongside: Unity 7 was unveiled at Unite Seoul (beta in Q4, full release Q1 2027), a multi-year Netflix games partnership was disclosed, and Create strategic revenue reached $157m, up 14% adjusted on price increases and China demand. Unity still trades at a fraction of AppLovin's EV/EBITDA multiple despite closing much of the growth gap — that spread is the re-rating case.
U.risk: Watch: AppLovin. The entire re-acceleration case rests on Vector holding ROAS parity or better against AXON, which has a multi-year data and scale head start and roughly 80% EBITDA margins to reinvest against Unity's 29%. Engine share is the second problem — Unreal out-earned Unity on Steam and leads developer mindshare, Godot absorbed the low end after the 2023 Runtime Fee episode, and Create remains the weak leg with cloud and hosting shrinking after the 2025 portfolio reset. Revenue is levered to cyclical mobile game advertising and in-app purchase spend and to platform policy, with Greater China around 18% of revenue. This is a high-beta momentum name that has already re-rated hard: take partial profits into strength, keep a stop ≈ 2× ATR below, and treat any sequential Vector deceleration below the guided 19-21% as the exit rather than a dip to add to.

SWK.business: Stanley Black & Decker makes and sells hand tools, power tools and outdoor equipment under DEWALT, CRAFTSMAN, STANLEY, BLACK+DECKER and CUB CADET, sold overwhelmingly through big-box home improvement retail — Home Depot is roughly 17% of net sales and Lowe's roughly 10%. A smaller Engineered Fastening business supplies rivets, threaded fasteners and assembly systems to automotive OEMs and Tier 1s such as Ford, GM, Stellantis and Bosch, and into general industry including data centres and solar. FY2025 net sales were $15.1bn, down 2%, with Tools & Outdoor at roughly 87% of the mix. The company sold its Consolidated Aerospace Manufacturing arm for $1.8bn in cash, closing in Q2 2026.
SWK.happening: Q2 2026, reported 29 July, showed power tools growing 8% organically — the fastest in several years — with adjusted EPS of $1.57 beating the guidance midpoint by $0.37 and adjusted gross margin expanding 620bps to 33.7%. FY26 adjusted EPS guidance moved to $5.20-5.80 (midpoint $5.50, +18% year over year) and free cash flow ex-CAM was lifted to $800m-$1.0bn from $500-700m.
SWK.why: Three drivers, with one important caveat. (1) The US commercial and industrial channel is doing the work: C&I grew low double digits and is on track to approach 10% of Tools & Outdoor sales this year, with DEWALT 'project solution managers' embedded on data-centre and power mega-projects running PERFORM & PROTECT safety training and on-site tool availability — a genuinely new demand pool for a company whose story has been big-box DIY. (2) Cash conversion improved materially, with the free cash flow guide raised $300m at both ends and the CAM divestiture adding $1.8bn to delever, while Engineered Fastening margin rose 220bps to 13% post-divestiture. (3) Management is claiming share gain rather than market recovery — Chris Nelson told Baird's Tim Wojs the 8% power-tool growth came from a multi-year go-to-market build, increased placement with key channel partners and promotions deliberately aligned to margin-accretive products. The caveat on earnings quality is important: roughly $0.37 of the beat came from below-the-line items and tariff refunds, and a $118m pre-tax IEEPA Phase 1 gain contributed ~250bps of the 620bps gross margin expansion, which management is recycling into field sales, trade specialists and new products rather than banking. At the $5.50 FY26 EPS midpoint SWK sits in the mid-teens on forward earnings, a discount to Techtronic and Snap-on, and that gap is the entire value case.
SWK.risk: Watch: the 2026 margin story is a refund-funded bridge. Guidance assumes new Section 301 tariffs land near prior rates, neutralising the temporary Section 122 tailwind, while battery metals, tungsten and oil each cost roughly $100m this year — and CFO Patrick Hallinan said 'it appears more likely than not a price increase will be necessary by 2027', which has not yet been tested with the channel. The mix underneath the headline is uneven: Outdoor fell 7% on weather, Hand Tools/Accessories/Storage grew only 2% and Europe declined 2% on France, so the full-year organic guide is still only low single digits despite the 8% power-tool print. Techtronic's Milwaukee has taken professional-trade share for a decade at better margins, and Home Depot and Lowe's — not Stanley — set shelf space and promotional pricing. Keep this a modest, value-tilted position sized for a slow turnaround: use a stop ≈ 2× ATR below entry, and treat a failed 2027 price increase or a Section 301 reset above assumed rates as the thesis-breaker.

ROKU.business: Roku licenses and operates the Roku OS, the software layer running on its own streaming players and on TVs built by TCL, Hisense and Sharp, reaching over 100 million global streaming households. It sells hardware deliberately at negative gross margin as a customer-acquisition cost, then monetises the installed base through home-screen and in-app advertising, The Roku Channel, and revenue-share plus subscription billing on behalf of streaming services. Following a June 2026 segment recast the mix is roughly 51% Advertising, 37% Subscriptions and 12% Devices, with about 88% of monetisation in the United States. Buyers are brand and performance CTV advertisers, streaming services paying for distribution and remote buttons, and retail consumers.
ROKU.happening: This is not a fundamentals breakout — it is merger arbitrage, and it should be sized as such. Fox Corporation agreed in June 2026 to acquire Roku for $160 per share ($96 cash plus 0.9693 Fox Class A shares), roughly $22bn enterprise value, with close expected in 1H 2027 subject to antitrust and shareholder approval. Roku has since stopped running the earnings machinery entirely: no Q2 2026 call and no guidance were given on 6 August 2026. The last standalone datapoint was Q1 2026 on 30 April, where platform revenue grew 28% and the FY26 platform guide went up over $100m to nearly 21% growth.
ROKU.why: The bull mechanism is deal arithmetic plus a decent stub. (1) A definitive agreement at $160 with a fixed $96 cash component bounds the downside to break economics rather than to the CTV ad cycle, and the return is simply the spread divided by time to a 1H 2027 close. (2) The remaining equity beta sits in the 0.9693 Fox Class A component, so the variable leg tracks Fox shares, not Roku's P&L — this is a two-asset position whether the holder intends it or not. (3) The underlying fundamentals still support the price if the deal breaks: advertising revenue grew 27% with advertising gross margin above 60%, up over 400bps and called sustainable; subscription revenue grew 30% (23% ex-Frndly) with Apple TV added in March and Peacock announced; free cash flow is again expected to exceed adjusted EBITDA. (4) The structural asset is real — Roku owns the first screen in ~100m households and takes roughly 44% of US CTV viewing hours, and made its authenticated inventory exclusively addressable through Amazon DSP, converting its largest OS rival into a distribution channel.
ROKU.risk: Watch: antitrust and shareholder approval are both unresolved, and a Fox-Roku combination invites real scrutiny of CTV inventory and ad-demand concentration — a second request would push the timeline out and widen the spread. The 0.9693 Fox Class A leg is unhedged unless the holder shorts it, so a Fox de-rate directly cuts the realised price. Management has stopped guiding and stopped hosting calls, so a break leaves you owning an unguided asset with a Devices segment that has run negative gross margin every year since 2021, Amazon DSP counterparty concentration, and Samsung, LG and Walmart-owned Vizio subsidising rival ad-funded TV operating systems. Size this as an arb sleeve, not a momentum position — cap it, hedge the Fox leg if you can, and accept that a break resets the stock toward pre-announcement levels, which is where the honest stop sits.

TEAM.business: Atlassian sells subscription software that engineering, IT and increasingly general business teams use to plan and track work — Jira for issue tracking, Confluence for documentation, Jira Service Management for IT service desks, plus Loom, Bitbucket, Trello and the Rovo AI layer. Over 300,000 customers buy it, historically through self-serve signup rather than a field sales force, though more than 500 now spend over $1m a year. FY2026 revenue was roughly $6.6bn, up 28%, with subscription ARR of $6.61bn; the mix is 69% cloud, 25% Data Center and 6% Marketplace. Buyers are software engineering organisations, ITSM teams, and now non-technical departments via the Teamwork Collection.
TEAM.happening: Atlassian reported Q4 FY2026 on 6 August 2026 and the stock moved roughly 35% after hours. Cloud growth re-accelerated to 31% and RPO jumped 44% to $4.8bn — commitments running well ahead of reported revenue. The twist is that management paired that with its first-ever full-year ARR guide, calling for about 18% FY27 subscription ARR growth against the 23% it had just printed, and spent the call defending the gap as prudence rather than deceleration. The buy side clearly read the 18% as a sandbag, which is exactly what the move implies.
TEAM.why: (1) The commitment build is the cleanest signal: RPO +44% to $4.8bn with FY27 cloud revenue growth guided at ~25.5%, so the revenue line is following bookings that are already banked. (2) AI is being monetised through edition and seat upgrades rather than a separate SKU — Rovo is used by over 80% of the Fortune 500, Rovo-assisted actions grew 50% sequentially, Rovo adopters expand ARR at more than twice the rate of non-adopters, and the Atlassian MCP server plus Teamwork Graph CLI passed one million monthly actives after doubling in a single quarter. (3) The Teamwork Graph is the structural moat behind that — over 200 billion objects and connections, with grounded agents delivering up to 44% more accurate answers on 48% fewer tokens, which Cannon-Brookes says is now a top-two stated reason customers upgrade to cloud. (4) Enterprise expansion set records at the $1m, $3m and $5m deal levels, with 164 customers above $3m ARR (+50% y/y) and 69 above $5m (+70% y/y), NRR above 120%, and Google Cloud cited as a system-of-work reference. (5) The 18% guide laps roughly one point of FY26 DX acquisition benefit and embeds extra H2 FY27 caution — a low bar deliberately set on the first-ever ARR guide.
TEAM.risk: Watch: the 23%-to-18% ARR step-down may be real deceleration rather than prudence — Data Center revenue is guided down about 17%, the migration tailwind contributed only mid-to-high single digits to cloud growth in FY26 and is now largely spent, so cloud has to carry the company on net-new seats and cross-sell. Seat-based pricing is levered to software engineering headcount, which AI coding agents are explicitly designed to reduce, and Microsoft bundles GitHub, Planner and Teams into E5 agreements CIOs already own. Rovo was given away inside existing paid tiers, so AI adoption shows up as cost of goods before it shows up as price, against a FY27 GAAP operating margin guide of only 4.5%. After a ~35% gap, do not chase — build on a pullback toward the gap fill and trail a stop under the earnings-gap low.

ELF.business: e.l.f. Beauty designs mass-market colour cosmetics and skincare, outsources nearly all manufacturing to third-party factories in China, and sells through Target, Walmart, Ulta, Amazon and its own e-commerce at price points 60-80% below prestige equivalents. The portfolio is e.l.f. Cosmetics, e.l.f. SKIN, Naturium, Well People, Keys Soulcare and rhode, the Hailey Bieber brand acquired in 2025. FY2026 net sales were $1.64bn, up about 25%, with roughly 79% of sales in the US and the top three retailers accounting for about 58% of the total. The edge is cycle time — concept to shelf in months versus two-plus years at Coty or L'Oreal.
ELF.happening: Q1 FY2027 landed on 5 August 2026 and reset the whole FY27 frame: rhode delivered $160m of net sales in a single quarter and a $50m tariff refund arrived, letting management lift FY27 sales growth guidance from 12-14% to 18-20% ($1.938-1.968bn), adjusted EBITDA growth to 20-21%, and adjusted EPS to $3.50-3.55. The catch is that organic net sales fell high single digits with units down about 3 points, so the raise is acquisition and refund optics layered over a soft core. Management simultaneously announced a pricing rollback after last August's $1 increase, having run a price-discovery test across most e.l.f. SKUs.
ELF.why: (1) rhode is a genuine growth engine, not a bolt-on: $160m of net sales ahead of internal plan, $27m of single-day sales on rhodeskin.com during the Summer of rhode launch bringing in 90,000 new customers, #1 ranking at Sephora North America, Sephora UK and Mecca — all achieved while sitting in under 20% of Sephora doors globally and with unaided awareness still only high single digits. (2) The distribution runway is dated and specific: rhode expands into Sephora across 19 European countries in September 2026, e.l.f. enters Sephora Brazil, and Naturium goes into Sephora Canada and Mexico. (3) The pricing reset is a volume fix — 90% of SKUs revert to pre-increase levels while the 10% that showed outsized unit response stay permanently lower, which Amin argues grows gross profit dollars outright on volume, and scanner-data dollar and unit trends are already improving. (4) Category and geography expansion compounds it: e.l.f. Hair launched exclusively at Target with six SKUs at $10 or less into a $17bn US category with nearly half of buyers new to e.l.f., international sales grew 61% to 21% of the total, and Boots and Dollar General space expanded. (5) Supply chain moves to 60% non-China production by FY27 exit, structurally cutting the tariff beta that just paid a $50m refund.
ELF.risk: Watch: organic net sales fell high single digits with units down about 3 points, so the core e.l.f. brand is not yet fixed, and the 6-7% FY27 organic guide requires a second-half inflection that has not printed. Q1's 83% gross margin included 10.5 points from refunds and is emphatically not a run rate — Fields disclosed the entire $50m tariff refund lands in Q1 but gets reinvested across Q2-Q4, netting to zero on the year, so the EBITDA raise has to come from the core. rhode is celebrity-dependent, a key-person risk on an $800m acquisition where creator-led brands historically have short half-lives, and retailer concentration means one planogram reset at Target, Walmart or Ulta is a material revenue event. Take a partial position now and add only on evidence of organic turning; use the Q2 FY27 print as the falsification point and stop out if organic growth does not inflect.

GTLB.business: GitLab sells a single application covering the whole software lifecycle — source control, code review, CI/CD pipelines, security scanning, package registry and the GitLab Duo AI layer — priced per seat across Free, Premium ($29) and Ultimate ($99) tiers. Unlike GitHub it ships a fully-featured self-managed edition, which is why regulated, air-gapped and government customers buy it, including via FedRAMP-authorised GitLab Dedicated for Government. FY2026 revenue was $955.2m, up 26%, with ARR crossing $1bn and 1,456 customers above $100k ARR. Buyers are enterprise platform engineering teams, banks, defence and healthcare, and US federal agencies.
GTLB.happening: On 2 June 2026 GitLab beat and raised while simultaneously announcing 'Act 2' — a 14% workforce cut (~350 employees), removal of up to three management layers, exit from 22 countries cutting the geographic footprint 37%, and a pivot from pure seats toward consumption pricing. The FY27 revenue guide went to $1.112-1.118bn (+16-17%) and non-GAAP operating income to $135-141m, absorbing $30-35m of restructuring charges. The Duo Agent platform, in its first quarter, reached nearly $20m of paid consumption run rate — explicitly guided to contribute no material FY27 revenue, which is the setup: the number is real and it is not in the model.
GTLB.why: (1) Duo Agent is the direct answer to the AI-kills-seats bear case — in its first quarter it added more net-new ARR than Duo Pro and Duo Enterprise combined in any prior period, hit ~$20m of paid consumption run rate, and GitLab Credits plus the new Flex buying program move the revenue model off seat count entirely. (2) Act 2 is self-help with a hard number attached: 14% of headcount and 37% of the country footprint removed, most savings redirected into R&D, AI tooling and strategic talent, which is why FY27 operating income rose even while carrying $30-35m of charges. (3) Enterprise anchors hold — GitLab Dedicated passed $70m ARR with multi-year commitments from Zillow Group and CSL, and Ultimate is 57% of ARR including seven of the top ten deals. (4) The partnership structure removes the budget-approval step: expanded AWS, Google Cloud and Anthropic relationships let customers spend existing cloud commits on Duo Agent, alongside an announced 'generational rebuild of Git' with an AI lab targeting 100x scale. (5) Persistent strategic interest in the asset gives the equity an option-like floor that pure execution names do not have.
GTLB.risk: Watch: revenue quality is running a step ahead of underlying commitments — total RPO grew only 18% against cRPO at 24%, and CFO Ross flagged $2m of nonrecurring overages and early renewals flattering reported revenue, right as Act 2 disruption begins. Staples flatly rejected the seat-compression premise ('actually, we've seen seats growing this quarter') while Ross separately conceded a price-sensitive cohort worth roughly 20% of ARR remains under pressure, so the erosion is real but concentrated. Profitability is guided to trough in Q3 FY27 on post-restructuring investment timing, GitHub Copilot is bundled into Microsoft agreements CIOs already own, and reports of OpenAI building AI-native code hosting reopened the durability question in March 2026. Half position at most, and treat the Q2 FY27 print as the falsification point — if seats or cRPO roll over post-restructuring, exit rather than average down.

DINO.business: HF Sinclair is an inland US refiner running roughly 678,000 barrels per day across seven plants — Puget Sound (149k), El Dorado KS (135k), Tulsa (125k), Navajo/Artesia (100k), Parco/Sinclair WY (94k), Woods Cross (45k) and Casper (30k). It also owns the Sinclair retail brand feeding about 1,600 branded stations, the former Holly Energy Partners pipeline and terminal network, a renewable diesel business, and a lubricants arm comprising Petro-Canada Lubricants, Sonneborn and Red Giant. Buyers are wholesale rack and jobber fuel purchasers across the Rockies and Mid-Continent, branded retail dealers, and industrial and pharmaceutical lubricants and white-oil accounts.
DINO.happening: Q2 2026, reported 28 July, was an outlier quarter — adjusted EBITDA more than doubled to $1.5bn on an unusually tight refining market, with refining segment EBITDA of $1.0bn (up 110%), lubricants at $207m versus $55m a year ago, and renewables swinging to $123m from a $2m loss. Two days later, on 30 July 2026, management announced a tax-efficient spin-off of Lubricants & Specialties as a separate public company within 12-18 months, and raised the quarterly dividend 5% to $0.525. Myers framed it plainly: 'we're not losing something, we're just splitting it among the stockholders.'
DINO.why: (1) The refining cycle is genuinely tight and management is underwriting it into next year — Myers cited Ukraine and Middle East disruptions, low inventories and limited new supply, stating outright 'we expect to have tighter refining markets as well into 2027', with 640 kbpd retained as an aspirational run level. (2) The lubricants spin is a sum-of-the-parts unlock that management now owns publicly: a segment printing $207m of quarterly adjusted EBITDA gets separated from the refining conglomerate discount as a tax-efficient spin rather than a sale, and Myers explicitly argued the more stable earnings stream should command a higher standalone multiple. (3) Capital return is scaling with the cycle — the dividend rose 5% to $0.525 with the roughly 50%-of-free-cash-flow return framework unchanged and FY26 capex guidance held flat, against a $1.5bn EBITDA quarter. (4) The structural edge is location: Rockies and Mid-Continent plants sit in supply-short, pipeline-constrained markets where imports cannot easily land, and can run discounted Uinta waxy and Canadian heavy barrels coastal refiners cannot access, so realised cracks run above Gulf Coast benchmarks. (5) Free options sit on top — pending small refinery exemptions, and Go-West pipeline phase-one FID targeted by end-2026 with possible 2029 startup.
DINO.risk: Watch: Q3 crude runs are guided down to 590-620 kbpd from 640 kbpd on the September El Dorado turnaround, so the sequential comparison gets worse before the spin lands. Management said small refinery exemption petitions remain pending and it expects relief 'soon' in at least one case while warning the RIN bank could end the year negative or only slightly balanced — compliance cost is the main unhedged downside inside an otherwise upgraded 2027 outlook, and the guide assumes policy help that has not arrived. The spin carries 12-18 months of execution risk, includes retiring the Mississauga base-oil refinery in favour of third-party supply agreements, and leaves RemainCo more exposed to the refining cycle, not less; crack spreads are entirely outside management control, and Q4 2025 alone carried a $313m lower-of-cost-or-market inventory charge. Trade this as a cyclical sized to the crack spread, not a compounder — stop out on a decisive rollover in Mid-Con and Rockies margins rather than on spin headlines.

WDAY.business: Workday runs the HR and finance system of record for large enterprises — payroll, benefits, recruiting and workforce planning in HCM, and general ledger, procurement and planning in Financial Management — delivered as a single multi-tenant cloud with two mandatory upgrades a year. It bills a subscription per worker under multi-year contracts to more than 11,500 organisations, over 7,000 of which run both HCM and Financials. FY2026 revenue was $9.55bn, up 13.1%, of which $8.83bn was subscription, at a 29.6% non-GAAP operating margin. Buyers are Fortune 500 HR and finance organisations, healthcare systems, universities and government agencies, with Deloitte, Accenture, PwC and Kainos as the implementation bench.
WDAY.happening: Q1 FY2027, reported 21 May 2026, delivered the best Q1 new-ACV growth in five years with agentic AI ARR approaching $500m and agentic new ACV up over 200% — and the stock fell about 3.5%, because Bhusri immediately damped it ('one quarter does not make a year', some of it Q4 slippage) and the FY27 subscription guide was reiterated at $9.925-9.95bn rather than raised. Only the margin guide moved, to 30.5%. That is the entire setup into the Q2 FY27 print in late August 2026: the bookings strength is visible, the guide is not, and Rowe flagged that flex-credit bookings ramp through the year with the larger impact landing in FY28 revenue.
WDAY.why: (1) Agentic AI is already monetising at scale — ARR approaching $500m, new ACV from agentic products up over 200%, 20 agents in GA or early access, customer adoption more than doubling sequentially past 4,000 customers, AI present in over 25% of expansion new ACV, and AI-attached expansion deals averaging over 50% larger. (2) Sana becomes the default Workday front end: Sana for Workday and the self-service agent were provisioned by end of May to all HCM and finance customers under existing contracts, with Sana founder Joel Hellermark named Chief AI Officer and Sana Travel Agent and Sana for ITSM extending Workday into adjacent spend categories. (3) Margin is coming from AI rather than headcount — headcount flat at 20,800 with the deployment agent targeting a ~30% reduction in implementation hours today and up to 50% in the next wave, FY27 non-GAAP operating margin guided to 30.5%, operating cash flow held at $3.45bn and free cash flow at $3.18bn (+15%). (4) Distribution is widening: EMEA medium-enterprise new ACV grew over 50%, partners sourced roughly 30% of net new ACV, EU data residency launched in Frankfurt and Workday entered Vietnam. (5) The replacement economics remain punitive — an 18-24 month reimplementation across payroll, benefits carriers and the GL — which is why the installed base funds the AI transition rather than shopping it.
WDAY.risk: Watch: per-worker pricing is directly levered to white-collar headcount, and Workday is selling agents explicitly on doing work that reduces the seats it bills for — the conversion of ~$500m of agentic ARR into subscription revenue is unproven, and management pointedly refused to raise the FY27 subscription guide off its best Q1 in five years. Sana was bundled into existing contracts as the de facto default front end with no incremental line item, so adoption is being bought now and monetisation deferred to a later cycle. Competitively, SAP's RISE bundles SuccessFactors with full ERP at migration discounts, Oracle already leads HR software share, Financial Management attach into the HCM base has lagged management's own targets, and federal, higher-education and healthcare deal cycles have elongated. At 13% growth this is a margin story carrying a growth multiple — size it accordingly, and use another reiterated-not-raised subscription guide at Q2 FY27 as the stop trigger.

RBRK.business: Rubrik sells cyber-resilience software: it backs up enterprise data from on-prem servers, cloud workloads and SaaS apps into an immutable, append-only store that is logically air-gapped from the customer's Active Directory, then detects ransomware and restores fast after an attack. It is deliberately sold to the CISO as a security control rather than to IT as backup, so it is funded from the security budget rather than the infrastructure budget. Go-to-market is almost entirely through channel partners and GSIs, into large enterprise, US federal (FedRAMP), financial services and healthcare. FY26 (to 31-Jan-2026) revenue was $1.32bn, up ~48%, with subscription ARR of $1.46bn and net retention above 120%.
RBRK.happening: Q1 FY27, reported 4-Jun-2026, put subscription ARR at $1.57bn, up 32%, with cloud now 89% of the mix and free cash flow more than doubling to $74m. The re-rating driver is cash: FY27 free cash flow is guided to $293m-$303m, turning a loss-making growth story into a self-funding one. Identity Resilience crossed $50m of subscription ARR after 38% quarter-over-quarter growth, and Rubrik Agent Cloud, built on the Predibase acquisition and paired with Anthropic's Project Glasswing, landed early production deployments in regulated financial services for policy-based agent governance and 'agent rewind' remediation.
RBRK.why: (1) The ARR base is high quality and compounding: 2,946 customers above $100K subscription ARR, up 24%, now represent 88% of subscription ARR, with NRR around 120% and FY27 subscription ARR guided to $1.854bn-$1.862bn (+27%). (2) Cash flow has inflected — $74m of FCF in Q1 alone against an FY27 guide of $293m-$303m, with Q2 subscription ARR contribution margin guided to 11-12%. (3) Second products are landing rather than being promised: Identity Resilience is past $50m ARR growing 38% sequentially, and Agent Cloud extends the CISO wallet beyond backup into agent governance. (4) The buying frame has moved onto Rubrik's turf, with CEO Sinha citing a 50% sequential increase in CIO and CISO resilience conversations as budget shifts from prevention and detection toward recovery.
RBRK.risk: Watch: headline revenue growth decelerates from 39% by design as material-rights revenue from the cloud migration winds down to just $17m for all of FY27 and $3m-$4m in Q2 — expect optically ugly prints where ARR is fine but reported growth halves. Cohesity (merged with Veritas NetBackup) and Veeam, which is preparing its own listing, both have larger installed bases to fund competitive spend, while AWS and Azure native backup commoditise the low end. Rubrik is still deeply GAAP-loss-making with heavy stock-based comp, so the multiple rests entirely on 27%+ ARR growth holding. Size it as a high-beta position; a cut to the $1.854bn-$1.862bn FY27 ARR guide or NRR slipping below 115% breaks the thesis — stop below the pre-Q1 base.

ESTC.business: Elastic commercialises Elasticsearch, the open-source distributed search and analytics engine that also serves as a vector database, packaged into three paid solutions: Search AI for application search and RAG retrieval, Observability for logs/metrics/APM, and Security for SIEM and endpoint. Customers either self-manage the software under a paid licence or buy consumption-based Elastic Cloud, which is 48% of revenue. Roughly 24,000 customers, of which 1,720+ spend over $100K annually and 240+ over $1m, including Uber, Cisco, Booking.com, Verizon and US federal agencies. FY26 (to 30-Apr-2026) revenue was $1.74bn, up 17%, with subscriptions at 94% of the total.
ESTC.happening: In the Q4 FY26 print on 28-May-2026 the commitment build mattered more than the beat: CRPO accelerated to 20% and RPO to 28%, far ahead of the ~14.6% FY27 revenue guide, because the Q4 mix skewed toward cloud where revenue ramps rather than being recognised upfront. Federal SIEM-as-a-Service with CISA has already exceeded its previously announced $26m twelve-month commitment as more civilian agencies switch off competitive security offerings. Elastic paired that with a margin story it raised twice over: FY27 non-GAAP operating margin guided to ~19% from 16.4%, and the FY29 medium-term target lifted from >20% to approximately 25%.
ESTC.why: (1) Commitments lead revenue by construction — 20% CRPO and 28% RPO growth against a $1.985bn-$2.0bn FY27 revenue guide (+14.6%) is a deployment-model artefact, and management said the guide embeds an accelerating trajectory from a low Q1 up to Q4. (2) Margin compounds independently of growth: 16.4% to ~19% in FY27, 21.5% adjusted FCF margin, and a raised ~25% FY29 target. (3) Security is the displacement engine — CISA over-consuming its $26m commitment, plus an eight-figure Fortune 50 financial-services SIEM displacement, is the evidence the federal win replicates commercially. (4) The context-platform pivot has real proof points rather than slideware: Agent Builder now GA, first-party Jina v5 Omni multimodal models, third-party connectors pulling live context from Slack and Google Drive without indexing, a published 70% token reduction versus naive RAG, and over 600 customers above $100K ACV using AI capabilities.
ESTC.risk: Watch: AWS OpenSearch is a free managed fork of Elastic's own engine and structurally caps cloud pricing power, while net expansion at 112% sits below software peers. The Q1 FY27 guide is deliberately the low print of the year at $469m-$470m (+13.1%) with ~14% operating margin — if the promised back-half acceleration has not shown by Q2/Q3, the CRPO-leads-revenue argument collapses into ordinary deceleration. Consumption revenue on Elastic Cloud is also volatile quarter to quarter as customers tune log retention and ingest to cut cost, and observability is a two-front war against Datadog and Cisco/Splunk, both of which outspend Elastic on go-to-market. Position moderately; the falsifier is a quarter where CRPO growth falls back toward the revenue growth rate.

THC.business: Tenet runs two very different businesses. Hospital Operations owns 49 acute-care and specialty hospitals, roughly 135 outpatient sites and the Conifer revenue-cycle JV, concentrated in Texas, Florida, California and Arizona. Ambulatory Care is USPI, the largest US ambulatory surgery centre operator, with interests in 533 ASCs (401 consolidated) and 26 surgical hospitals across 37 states, mostly structured as joint ventures with roughly 6,000 owner-surgeons. Payers are commercial managed care (UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Cigna, Elevance), Medicare and Medicare Advantage, and state Medicaid directed-payment programs. FY25 revenue was $21.31bn with adjusted EBITDA of $4.57bn.
THC.happening: Q2 2026, reported 24-Jul-2026, was a clean beat-and-raise: FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance lifted $295m at the midpoint to $4.83bn-$5.03bn, revenue up $300m to $21.9bn-$22.5bn, and $1.04bn of stock repurchased in the quarter. What makes it a breakout is what it absorbed — exchange revenue fell 17% and exchange admissions 13.5%, a quantified $65m Q2 revenue headwind, and Tenet raised anyway. Hospital segment EBITDA margin went from 15.6% to 18.0% on a three-bucket cost program running since 1-Jan-2026.
THC.why: (1) The ACA enhanced-subsidy expiry is an already-underwritten ~$250m 2026 adjusted EBITDA headwind concentrated in the hospital segment — management assumes 20% exchange enrolment attrition and near one-for-one conversion of exchange patients into uninsured, and CFO Sun Park explicitly declined to change the H2 assumption, so the $295m raise is pure operating upside sitting on top of the hit rather than a re-forecast of payer mix. (2) The cost program — purchased-services renegotiation, clinical ops (length of stay, ED throughput, OR and cath-lab utilization) and AI/automation through the offshore Global Business Center — delivered 240bps of hospital margin in two quarters. (3) USPI acuity migration is doing the work volume used to: net revenue per case +6.3% against a deliberate 1.2% case-volume decline, with 10% same-store growth in ASC total joint replacements and general-surgical robotics scaling. (4) The balance sheet funds the equity — leverage 2.33x, $2.1bn cash, no revolver borrowings, no significant maturities until late 2027, $2.13bn of buyback authorization remaining and FY26 adjusted FCF after NCI guided to $1.825bn-$2.055bn.
THC.risk: Watch: the ~$250m subsidy hit is a 2026 number — if enhanced subsidies stay expired into 2027 the uninsured conversion compounds into next year's base rather than lapping clean, and bad debt follows it. State Medicaid supplemental and directed-payment pools are a large, non-recurring-feeling earnings contributor subject to CMS approval and reauthorisation, while anesthesia and nursing cost inflation lands directly on ASC margins and staffing shortages can idle profitable ORs. Optum/SCA is buying ASC capacity as a vertically integrated payer-provider, so it is simultaneously a competitor and a counterparty setting Tenet's reimbursement. Own it as a cash-return compounder rather than a growth name; the falsifier is a 2027 guide that fails to grow EBITDA off the raised 2026 base, or a Medicaid directed-payment disallowance.

EXPE.business: Expedia Group runs the world's second-largest online travel marketplace, taking a cut of hotel, home-rental, flight and car bookings made on Expedia, Hotels.com, Vrbo, Orbitz, Travelocity and Hotwire. Increasingly it sells the same supply and booking technology wholesale through the Rapid API and white-label sites, so Chase's Ultimate Rewards portal, Delta Stays and corporate travel agencies can sell travel without owning inventory — B2B is roughly a third of revenue across ~75,000 partners and ~200,000 travel advisors. It also sells advertising against its traffic (EG Advertising, $758m FY25) and through trivago metasearch. FY25 revenue was $14.73bn on $119.6bn of gross bookings.
EXPE.happening: Q2 2026, reported 5-Aug-2026, was the fifth straight quarter above the high end of guidance — bookings +12%, revenue +14%, EBITDA +23% — on the strongest US consumer demand in 15 quarters, with longer stays and longer booking windows. FY26 guidance went up across the board: gross bookings to $129.5bn-$130.8bn, revenue to $16.05bn-$16.22bn, and adjusted EBITDA margin expansion to +150-175bps. B2B posted its 20th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, the Tiqets acquisition closed in Q2, and management announced its intent to acquire CarTrawler to add B2B car rental and insurance.
EXPE.why: (1) The US point of sale is 59% of revenue and the highest-margin part of the book, and it has inflected after two soft years — that single variable swings the model more than anything else. (2) B2B is the structural growth engine and the actual moat: 20 straight double-digit quarters, roughly 21 billion API calls a day, and switching costs that make an embedded bank or airline portal sticky in a way consumer brands re-bought with paid marketing never are; Tiqets and CarTrawler extend a lodging-heavy book into full trip components. (3) Operating leverage runs deeper than the marketing reset — overheads were flat year over year on +14% revenue, driving +23% EBITDA. (4) AI is being run as offence: conversion-accretive ranking and personalisation already live in the core funnel, Vrbo natural-language search and Property Expert yielding 60%+ more traveler-intent data, and on distribution Expedia is an early adopter of ChatGPT's ad product, expanded across Google's AI surfaces and bought the Layla trip-planning app.
EXPE.risk: Watch: CFO Derek Anderson conceded Expedia begins lapping last year's marketing cuts in H2, flagged FX and B2B investment as Q3 drags, and the FY guide implies only ~50bps of Q4 margin expansion at the midpoint — 2027 expansion has to come from structural efficiency, not another cost reset. Google AI Mode and agentic booking assistants sit squarely on the one-third of traffic Expedia pays for, and CEO Ariane Gorin is deliberately refusing to size that channel, calling it 'still a small channel'. Vrbo keeps losing alternative-accommodation share to Airbnb, and the B2B mix shift is structurally dilutive at ~26% segment EBITDA margin versus ~30% for B2C. Trim into strength rather than adding; the falsifier is a Q3 miss on the guided 32.5-32.8% EBITDA margin or US room-night growth rolling back over.
