CCC.business: CCC sells the software a US auto insurance claim actually runs on. When a car is damaged, the adjuster, body shop, parts supplier and OEM all work off a CCC estimate and exchange documents, photos, parts orders and payments across CCC's cloud network — 300+ carriers including 18 of the 20 largest US auto insurers, 30,500+ collision repair facilities and 6,000+ parts suppliers. Revenue is roughly 85% fixed subscription per seat or per carrier rather than per claim, plus transaction fees on parts and repair workflow. EvolutionIQ, acquired in 2025, extends the model into disability and workers' comp claims AI and now into auto casualty via MedHub. FY25 revenue was $1.057bn, up 12%, at a 41% adjusted EBITDA margin.
CCC.happening: Q2 2026, reported 30-Jul-2026, cleared the high end of guidance on both revenue and EBITDA, and AI solutions crossed $120m of annualized revenue growing ~45-50% — about 11% of total and roughly 4 points of the quarter's 10% growth, led by APD, subrogation and EvolutionIQ. The stock still fell 8.4% premarket, because the implied Q4 exit rate of ~9% and CFO Katie Coleman's explicit refusal to guide 2027 told investors AI is not yet enough to re-rate the growth algorithm. FY26 revenue was narrowed with the midpoint slightly raised to $1.158bn-$1.164bn and adjusted EBITDA guided to $485m-$491m at roughly a 42% margin. That setup — a clean beat sold off on a guidance refusal — is precisely the disconnect the breakout is closing.
CCC.why: (1) AI has crossed from pilot to scale business: >$120m annualized at ~11% of revenue, growing ~45-50%, and now the majority of incremental growth, with CCC's largest AI-enabled subrogation carrier win to date landing in the quarter. (2) The go-to-market has two shots per customer, not one — President Tim Wells described carriers adding AI modules at core-platform renewal AND mid-cycle, evidenced by a top-5 carrier that renewed all core solutions, layered on the full AI suite, then added subrogation in Q2. (3) The moat is unusually hard: the CCC estimate is the document the insurer pays against and the shop bills against, software gross dollar retention runs around 99%, and two decades of parts pricing, labour times and repair outcomes is the training data behind Estimate-STP and MedHub that no competitor can buy. (4) Margin is expanding into the growth — roughly 100bps of adjusted EBITDA expansion at the high end and stock-based comp guided down from 13% to 11-12% of revenue.
CCC.risk: Watch: the growth algorithm is the entire debate — organic went from 7% last year to a guided 10%, but H2 only normalizes to ~10% excluding a legacy first-party casualty customer roll-off that costs about a point, and management flatly would not underwrite 2027. Underneath the network the transaction base is structurally shrinking as ADAS lowers accident frequency and higher vehicle values push more accidents to total loss. The largest carriers building in-house AI estimating would cap the ~$120m AI upsell that is the whole growth narrative, and Q4 carries the margin load after Q2 expense timing slipped, which Coleman deflected on rather than defended. Keep it half-size; the falsifier is a Q3/Q4 miss on the implied ramp or a top-5 carrier loss to Solera or Enlyte/Mitchell.

JHX.business: James Hardie makes the exterior of a house: fiber cement siding and trim under the Hardie brand, composite and PVC decking and railing under TimberTech, AZEK and Versatex, and fermacell fiber gypsum boards in Europe. It sells through building-products distributors, lumber dealers and big-box retail to contractors and homebuilders, and makes money converting customers off pressure-treated wood and vinyl onto higher-priced engineered materials. Irish-incorporated, Chicago-headquartered and dual-listed on the NYSE and ASX, with North America at 77% of sales. FY26 (year to March 2026) net sales were $4.84bn, up 25% on the $8bn+ AZEK acquisition closed July 2025, though organic net sales fell 2%.
JHX.happening: The Q1 FY27 report on 6-Aug-2026 — the company's first quarter of the new fiscal year, not an FY26 result — was the inflection: North American fiber cement organic sales rose 20% with sell-through accelerating to +19% in June. A national distribution agreement with Boise Cascade effective 31-Jul-2026, carrying Hardie siding, AZEK Exteriors and TimberTech decking together for the first time, plus six major regional distributors, let management raise FY27 guidance on an unchanged housing macro assumption. FY27 net sales guidance went from $5.25bn-$5.41bn to $5.564bn-$5.723bn, and pro forma adjusted EBITDA growth from +4-8% to +7.4-13.7% ($1.536bn-$1.625bn).
JHX.why: (1) The distribution reset is the real unlock and is self-help independent of housing starts — Boise Cascade nationally plus six regionals now carrying the combined portfolio is what underpins the reaffirmed $125m commercial revenue synergy run-rate exit for FY27. (2) AZEK integration has moved from cost to operations: over half of targeted G&A synergies actioned, the Hardie Operating System extended across AZEK's manufacturing network, and the Fontana and Summerville closures delivering roughly $25m of annualized savings. (3) Price and mix are holding where they matter — Siding & Trim margin of 33.5%, up 140bps, on ~5.5 points of price plus ~0.5 point of ColorPlus mix, with multifamily now 15% of fiber cement volume. (4) Deleveraging is on schedule: $400m of senior unsecured notes redeemed early, net leverage 2.7x targeting ~2.4x by FY27-end and below 2x by FY28, with FY27 free cash flow reaffirmed above $500m on capex of 6-7% of sales.
JHX.risk: Watch: management itself quantified how much of the inflection is non-repeating — CEO Aaron Erter split the fiber cement +20% into roughly one-third destock comp ($40-50m), one-third initiatives and one-third price/mix, and guided the rest of FY27 price/mix down to only 3.5-4%, implying an underlying run-rate closer to mid-single digits. Implied second-half group EBITDA is down a couple of percent, which Erter defended as 'normal seasonality' and 'being prudent' — the raise is Q1 flow-through and new-distribution stocking, not a call that housing has turned. Note also that the EBITDA guide definition changed to exclude share-based comp (~$50m in the original FY27 guide, ~$15m booked in Q1), so the raise is smaller than it reads, against $4.49bn of debt and roughly $1.01bn of asbestos liability funded off operating cash flow. Size it as a cyclical with a self-help overlay; the falsifier is a Q2 FY27 print inside the $1.485bn-$1.575bn sales guide but with sell-through decelerating back to single digits.

MRNA.business: Moderna makes and sells vaccines built on messenger-RNA technology, which instructs the body's own cells to produce a target protein. Three products carry revenue today: Spikevax (original COVID shot), mNEXSPIKE (next-generation COVID shot launched in the US in 2025) and mRESVIA (RSV). Customers are national governments buying under multi-year supply agreements (UK, Canada, Australia, Mexico, Taiwan, Japan) plus the US retail pharmacy channel. Revenue has collapsed from the $19.3bn COVID peak to roughly $1.9bn in FY2025, so the equity is now a cash-runway-plus-pipeline story rather than a product story.
MRNA.happening: The stock is breaking out off a multi-year base as the narrative flips from COVID melt to platform optionality. Q2 2026 revenue of $145m cleared the top of Moderna's own guide, and management cut FY26 cost of sales from $1.8bn to $1.7bn and R&D from $3.0bn to $2.9bn while raising year-end cash guidance to $4.7-5.2bn. Two hard catalysts landed alongside it: mFLUSIVA (mRNA-1010) carried an Aug. 5, 2026 PDUFA date for what would be a fifth approval, and mNEXSPIKE took 24% of the US retail COVID market (34% in the 65+ cohort).
MRNA.why: The mechanism is a discount unwind, not a revenue inflection. (1) Cash-cost discipline has pushed the FY26 cash cost target to roughly $4bn ex-SBC and D&A against $4.7-5.2bn of year-end cash, which removes the runway-panic discount that compressed the multiple through 2025. (2) The revenue base has quietly moved offshore - 69% of H1 2026 revenue was international, anchored by a European Commission joint procurement for up to 24 million mRESVIA doses across six countries plus UK, Canada and Australia partnerships - which structurally dilutes the RFK Jr. HHS policy overhang that drove the 2025 derating. (3) Oncology has moved to the front of the pipeline: intismeran with Merck showed a 49% reduction in recurrence-or-death over five years in adjuvant melanoma with Phase III fully enrolled and an interim due in 2026. On valuation, the market has been capitalising Moderna close to its own cash balance, so the enterprise value ascribed to the entire platform is small versus BioNTech on a cash-adjusted basis - which is precisely why a single pipeline win reprices the equity disproportionately.
MRNA.risk: Watch: seasonal concentration is brutal - management guides roughly 55% of second-half 2026 revenue into Q3 alone, so one weak autumn campaign resets the year. Cash burn is still real (Q2 2026 net loss of $782m on $145m of revenue), mRNA-1010 needs a CDC/ACIP recommendation rather than just FDA approval to become a commercial market, and lipid-nanoparticle IP litigation (Alnylam, Arbutus/Genevant, GSK) leaves unresolved royalty exposure on the delivery technology. Management explicitly refused to discuss flu pricing or give any read-through on the mRNA-1403 norovirus interim, so launch economics are unmodelable in 2026. Size this small - it is a binary-event book, not a compounder - and stop below the breakout base rather than trying to hold through a readout.

CHYM.business: Chime is a US consumer fintech offering fee-free checking and savings, a debit card and a secured credit card to mass-market Americans; it is not a bank, with deposits held and cards issued by partner banks The Bancorp and Stride. Roughly 69% of revenue is interchange paid by merchants on every card swipe, and 31% comes from fee-based liquidity products - MyPay earned wage access, SpotMe overdraft and Instant Loans. The customer is a working American with recurring direct deposit, typically under $100k of income, though the new Chime Prime tier is deliberately pulling upmarket.
CHYM.happening: Q2 2026 was a clean guidance raise across every line: FY26 revenue lifted to $2.725-2.745bn (25-26% growth), adjusted EBITDA to $465-475m at a 17% margin, and net new active members from 1.4m to 1.8m. Management paired the beat with a 10% workforce reduction and the CFO's departure. Underneath, MyPay originated $4.5bn at a 0.9% loss rate with transaction profit more than tripling to $73m, and Instant Loans hit $300m, up roughly 70% sequentially.
CHYM.why: This is the quarter where the interchange-only bear case broke. (1) Monetisation per member is inflecting: blended ARPAM rose 6% to $260, Prime members (requiring $3,000/month of direct deposits) generate over 2x base ARPAM, and the $75k+ income segment is now the fastest-growing cohort - so the mix is moving away from the subprime label the market applied at IPO. (2) The credit stack is scaling with real funding behind it: a new $500m Goldman Sachs warehouse facility supports a Prime-gated revolving line of credit, ring-fencing new credit risk to the highest-deposit cohort where Chime sits at the top of the repayment stack. (3) Operating leverage is now structural - a 10% headcount cut on top of roughly 10% annual cost-to-serve reduction in each of the last four years turns 25% revenue growth into the first GAAP-profitable year. On valuation, Chime trades at a materially lower EV/sales than the high-growth fintech cohort despite 25%+ growth, and unlike SoFi - whose balance sheet exceeds $10bn - the Durbin small-bank exemption preserves roughly 1.5% per debit swipe versus about 0.05% for a capped issuer.
CHYM.risk: Watch: the Durbin exemption is the single point of failure - any repeal or change to the $10bn partner-bank asset threshold hits roughly two-thirds of revenue directly, and Bancorp/Stride concentration is an existential operating dependency. Management explicitly guided MyPay loss rates higher in Q3 and Q4 after raising limits to $1,000, saying they optimise for transaction profit rather than loss rate, so credit optics deteriorate on purpose and the market may misread it as cycle stress. The CFO seat is open, guidance of $465-475m adjusted EBITDA has no cushion for a miss, and post-IPO venture supply from the June 2025 listing remains an overhang. Half position at most until a permanent CFO is named; stop below the breakout pivot.

CAI.business: Caris Life Sciences runs a precision-oncology laboratory. An oncologist sends a tumour sample; Caris runs whole-exome DNA and whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing (MI Profile, with FDA-approved MI Cancer Seek as the NGS component) plus a blood-based assay (Caris Assure), and returns a report matching the patient to therapies and trials. Medicare via MolDX is the effective price-setter for roughly 90% of revenue, and Caris separately licenses the resulting multi-omic database and AI models to pharma. About 92% of revenue is molecular profiling services, 8% pharma and research.
CAI.happening: Q2 2026 beat consensus revenue by 10.8% at $263.7m, up 45%, on a record 59,200 clinical cases and a record blended ASP above $3,850. Management raised FY26 revenue guidance from $1.00-1.02bn to $1.03-1.04bn. GAAP gross margin expanded to 68% from 63% a year ago, delivering a fifth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA ($55.7m) and free cash flow ($6.4m) even after $22.1m of capex, with roughly $18m repurchased under a $100m authorisation.
CAI.why: The breakout is a profitability-proof event on a name the market priced as a cash-burning IPO. (1) Price and mix are doing the work alongside volume: blended ASP above $3,850 with MI Cancer Seek covered lives at roughly 239.5 million and Caris Assure at roughly 131.9 million, which converts each incremental case into more revenue than it did a year ago. (2) The ordering channel has shifted decisively - 74% of orders now arrive through EHR and portal integration versus roughly 50% in Q1 2025 - which lowers customer acquisition cost and hard-wires Caris into the oncologist workflow against Tempus AI and Foundation Medicine, who compete precisely on that integration. (3) An entire product wave sits outside the guide: CFO Luke Power confirmed the raise is purely molecular profiling with zero contribution from Caris Detect (multi-cancer early detection across 58 cancer types from one blood draw, launched June 2026), ChromoSeq, MI Clarity V2 or the H2 2026 MRD assay - a deliberate sandbag that leaves 2027 as free option value. On valuation, Caris now trades on roughly $1.04bn of 2026 revenue with adjusted EBITDA and FCF already positive, whereas Tempus AI - the closest analogue on the data-plus-diagnostics model - is still not free-cash-flow positive, so Caris is arguably the cheaper asset on a cash-generation basis despite the higher growth rate.
CAI.risk: Watch: reimbursement concentration is the whole thesis - a MolDX rate revision or PAMA repricing of the comprehensive genomic profiling code hits roughly 90% of revenue with no offset, and Caris does not set the rate. The 2026 raise is mix- and price-led rather than volume-led (clinical volume guided up roughly 20% against 21-22% molecular profiling revenue growth), so it is not repeatable if per-test reimbursement normalises, and GAAP opex is guided up 19-20% against only just-achieved positive EBITDA. Caris Assure still needs its own ADLT or gap-fill decision before blood-based volume carries revenue, and the June 2025 IPO leaves founder control plus lockup supply. Size two-thirds normal given the single-payer dependency; stop below the pivot and cut on any MolDX rate headline.

FRO.OL.business: Frontline owns and operates large crude oil and refined-product tankers and rents them out, overwhelmingly on the spot market where the daily rate resets voyage by voyage. The fleet is roughly 80 owned vessels of about 17.6m dwt - VLCCs, Suezmaxes and LR2/Aframaxes - at 7.5 years average age, 100% eco-design and 64% scrubber-fitted, with a fleet-wide cash breakeven near $24,100/day. Customers are oil majors, national oil companies, Chinese and Indian refiners and commodity trading houses. Control sits with the Fredriksen family's Hemen Holding.
FRO.OL.happening: This is a Strait of Hormuz trade. Frontline earned $103,500/day on VLCCs in Q1 2026 and had already booked 82% of Q2 VLCC days at $181,700/day, with Suezmax at $131,300/day on 79% of days and LR2/Aframax at $125,000/day on 68% - six-figure TCE across every segment against a $24,100/day breakeven. The Q2 print, which will crystallise those rates into cash and a variable dividend, is due imminently.
FRO.OL.why: The move is arithmetic, not sentiment. (1) Realised rates are running at roughly seven times cash breakeven, which management translated into approximately $1.5bn or about $7 per share of annual cash generation - an 18% cash flow yield on the price at the time of the Q1 call - and Frontline pays the variable dividend straight out of quarterly cash flow, so the yield is delivered rather than promised. (2) The dislocation is tonne-mile rather than barrels: the initial Middle East Gulf supply loss cut the effective available fleet by only about 11 VLCC equivalents, but the long-haul substitution it forced redrew utilisation far enough that oil-on-water is back to pre-closure levels - a structurally longer voyage on the same cargo. (3) The balance sheet can hold the position through the volatility: $945m of cash and equivalents including a $473m undrawn revolver, no significant maturities until 2030, and nearly 30% of the next twelve months of VLCC days already fixed on time charter around $120,000/day on a steeply backwardated curve. On valuation, at these TCEs the equity trades at a low single-digit multiple of run-rate cash generation and below newbuild-parity asset value versus DHT and Okeanis, with a lower breakeven than either.
FRO.OL.risk: Watch: management is openly hedging against its own bull case. Barstad conceded he does not know why 55 VLCCs are sitting on standby outside the Arabian Gulf, then offered the theory that they are pre-positioned to move the moment someone tweets that Hormuz is reopening - an explicit admission the rate spike is fragile - and Frontline kept adding time-charter cover through the quarter, which is the tell that $180k/day is not underwritten as sustainable. OPEC+ cuts remove the highest-value long-haul barrels directly, a Russia sanctions relief scenario releases hundreds of shadow-fleet tankers into the compliant market overnight, and $925m of remaining newbuild commitments are being funded near the cycle top into 2027-28 deliveries. Trade this, do not hold it: half size, trail a stop under the breakout, and exit on any credible Hormuz de-escalation headline rather than waiting for the chart.

BLKB.business: Blackbaud sells the back-office software that nonprofits, private K-12 schools, universities and corporate giving programmes run on - donor CRM and fundraising (Raiser's Edge NXT), nonprofit accounting (Financial Edge NXT), school administration and tuition management, and corporate grantmaking (YourCause). Roughly 98% of revenue is recurring: 64% software subscriptions and 34% a transactional cut of every donation and tuition payment processed through Blackbaud's own payments rail. The customer base is tens of thousands of fragmented nonprofit and school accounts with no single material customer.
BLKB.happening: Q2 2026 printed at the high end of guidance - revenue $290.6m (+3.0% organic), non-GAAP EPS $1.33 (+9%) and free cash flow $75.3m, up 46% - and management steered investors to the top half of every FY26 range and to at or above the high end on both EPS and free cash flow, a raise in all but name. The capital-return engine is what changed the chart: 6.1% of shares were repurchased in H1 2026 alone, with 15% of shares retired since Q4 2023.
BLKB.why: The market is finally underwriting the algorithm rather than the growth rate. (1) Share-count compression is the earnings driver: over 50% of cumulative free cash flow is committed to buybacks through 2030 against $280-290m of FY26 FCF, so 4-6% organic growth mechanically compounds into double-digit EPS growth without a single incremental customer. (2) Contract duration has lengthened materially - 25% of contractual recurring revenue is now on four-year-plus terms, up from 20%, with 90% on three-year-plus - converting the churn debate into a contracted-backlog question. (3) The AI layer moved from demo to revenue-eligible: the fundraising development agent is out of the early-adopter programme and generally available, with four agent solutions in market and five new AI products launched or announced in 2026 carrying essentially zero revenue in guidance. On valuation, $5.15-5.25 of FY26 non-GAAP EPS and roughly $285m of FCF against a mid-cap market value puts BLKB at a low-teens earnings and free-cash multiple - a wide discount to vertical SaaS peers posting the same Rule of 40 (41% this quarter), because the market pays for growth and refuses to pay for share retirement. The rerate is the trade.
BLKB.risk: Watch: 3.0% organic growth is genuinely thin, and the Rule of 40 is being met through margin rather than growth - if the margin lever exhausts before growth reaccelerates the multiple caps out. Transactional revenue is directly levered to US charitable giving volume, which the Blackbaud Institute measured up only 4.3% in 2025, and to any change in the US charitable deduction; federal and state grant cuts squeeze the same customer budgets. Management routed all retention softness to a 2026 renewal cohort 40% larger than 2025 and promised normalisation only by end-2027, a two-year window in which the structural-churn debate cannot be settled by the data. Treat this as a slow compounder rather than a momentum add - full size is acceptable but expect a wide base; stop below the breakout pivot, not on noise.

PSX.business: Phillips 66 is a US downstream and midstream energy company. It refines crude into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, gathers and fractionates natural gas liquids and exports LPG from the Gulf Coast, sells fuel through roughly 7,000 US and 1,700 international Phillips 66, 76 and Conoco branded sites, owns half of petrochemical joint venture CPChem, and produces renewable diesel and SAF at Rodeo. Customers are branded wholesale marketers and dealers, Asian and European petrochemical crackers buying LPG, airlines and marine bunker buyers. Earnings swing violently with refining crack spreads - from $133m in Q3 2025 to $3.8bn in Q2 2026.
PSX.happening: Q2 2026 was the best quarter since 2022: $3.8bn of adjusted earnings and $9.41 EPS against roughly $7.02 consensus, on a $24.08/bbl realised refining margin at 96% crude utilisation and 86% clean product yield. Total debt was cut by $6.6bn to $20.6bn, with net debt at $16.5bn heading below $16bn by year-end against a $15bn total-debt target. Rodeo ran a record 106% utilisation for $544m of renewable fuels pre-tax income.
PSX.why: Management is explicitly underwriting a multi-year rather than multi-quarter upcycle, and the market is only now discounting it. (1) CEO Lashier drew a hard distinction on the call: 2022 was a demand shock that resolved once maintenance caught up, whereas today is a supply shock with capacity permanently offline and low stocks, so it takes far longer to normalise - a structurally higher mid-cycle crack. (2) The non-crack earnings legs are compounding independently: over 1 million bpd of NGL fractionation running above 100% utilisation, 943,000 bpd of NGL pipeline throughput, and a $4.5bn Midstream EBITDA run-rate target held for end-2027, on assets nobody can permit again. (3) Commercial has become a genuine third earner - the time-charter fleet expanded fourfold in two years and now supports roughly 40% of asset-backed demand, Phillips 66 took around 20% of all Jones Act waivers issued since March, and is now the third-largest buyer of Venezuelan crude worldwide. On valuation, PSX trades at a low single-digit multiple of annualised Q2 earnings and a mid-single-digit EV/EBITDA against Marathon Petroleum and Valero, with a midstream business that on a standalone $4.5bn EBITDA basis would be worth a large fraction of the current market cap - which is exactly why Elliott is still engaged with two board seats.
PSX.risk: Watch: a $24.08/bbl realised refining margin is far above mid-cycle and mean reversion is the base case, not the bear case. Management pre-emptively de-rated its own best segment on the call - the $544m renewable print was attributed largely to Iran-war-driven RIN and diesel strength plus a roughly $100m one-time tariff refund, and foreign-feedstock RIN generation may be halved after next year - while conceding China has around 2.5 million bpd of runs offline that could return as product exports. Q3 carries $100-120m of turnaround expense, a single unplanned Gulf Coast outage moves the quarter by hundreds of millions, and $20.6bn of total debt still competes with buybacks for the same cash. Buy the trend but scale out into crack-spread spikes rather than adding into them; stop below the breakout base.

WAWI.OL.business: Wallenius Wilhelmsen ships finished vehicles and rolling heavy equipment across oceans and then handles them on land. It runs around 128 RoRo and pure car and truck carriers on 15 trade lanes, plus roughly 70 vehicle processing centres, an inland trucking and rail network, eight marine terminals, and a US government sealift business (American Roll-on Roll-off Carrier). Revenue comes from multi-year contracts of affreightment with car makers and construction, mining and agricultural equipment manufacturers. FY2025 revenue was $5,240m with adjusted EBITDA of $1,811m and a contract backlog above $10bn.
WAWI.OL.happening: Q2 2026 saw management lift FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance from $1.6bn to $1.7bn on relentless Chinese vehicle exports and the best Logistics quarter in about five years ($46m segment adjusted EBITDA), even though extraordinary bunker costs pushed group adjusted EBITDA down 7% sequentially to $361m. The balance sheet transformed alongside it - the equity ratio jumped to 49% from 39% as the EUKOR liability fell, leverage sits at 1.2x, liquidity is $1.2bn and LTM ROCE is 15.6%. An H1 dividend of $0.61 per share, or $258m, was declared.
WAWI.OL.why: The market is repricing this from a cyclical car carrier to a contracted logistics asset. (1) The RoRo capacity shortage is structural rather than cyclical - roughly 2 million cars are currently moving in containers and possibly more than 1 million more via LoLo and dry bulk, all of which management expects to return to RoRo once capacity exists, so as CEO Kristoffersen put it, even with no growth out of China there will be growing demand for RoRo. (2) Contract quality is improving at the same time: Chinese OEMs are moving from transactional one-year deals to two-, three- and five-year contracts and asking for terminals, processing and end-to-end orchestration rather than just slots, which is what converts a shipping multiple into a logistics multiple, and underpins a backlog above $10bn against $5.2bn of annual revenue. (3) The dominant bear overhang is fading rather than crystallising - the USTR Section 301 fee of $46 per net tonne that management sized at $300-400m for 2026 has not shown up in the raised guide. On valuation, $1.7bn of FY26 EBITDA against 1.2x leverage and a $258m half-year dividend leaves the shares on a low single-digit EV/EBITDA and a high-single-digit dividend yield, broadly in line with Hoegh Autoliners but with a landside logistics network and a government sealift franchise that the pure carriers simply do not have.
WAWI.OL.risk: Watch: Section 301 is unresolved, not gone - management has still not received confirmation that the White House's November 2025 one-year suspension covers vehicle carriers, and the exposure is $300-400m for full-year 2026 if it does not. US auto import tariffs adding an estimated $4,000-6,000 per imported vehicle suppress exactly the Asia-to-US and Europe-to-US lanes that carry the best rates, the industry order book is roughly 21%, and Kristoffersen said there will sure be more to come beyond the 14-vessel Shaper Class - fleet growth is the mechanism that erodes today's scarcity premium. CFO Bukholm would only say Logistics has been lifted to a new level and refused to put a number on coming quarters. Size normally but treat the Sept. 24 market update as a hard checkpoint; stop below the breakout base and cut on an adverse Section 301 ruling.

WEX.business: WEX issues closed-loop fuel cards to commercial vehicle fleets (52% of revenue), administers HSA/FSA/COBRA benefit accounts with roughly $4.2bn of custodial deposits held inside its own Utah industrial bank (30%), and issues virtual cards for corporate accounts payable and online travel agencies (18%). It earns interchange on transaction value, per-vehicle and per-account servicing fees, finance charges on late-paying fleets, and net interest on the HSA float. Customers are fleet operators and government agencies, US employers, and OTAs; 88% of revenue is domestic.
WEX.happening: WEX printed a 52-week high of $203.99 on 24-25 August and sits at $199.71, about 20% above its 50-day moving average of $166.75 and 28% above the 200-day at $156.14. The 23 July Q2 print beat the high end of company guidance and management lifted FY26 to $2.86-2.90bn of revenue and $19.68-$20.08 adjusted EPS, a $19.88 midpoint versus $19.62 consensus. The completed BP portfolio migration flipped Mobility transaction growth from -2% to slightly positive, and leverage fell to 2.9x, inside the 2.5-3.0x target, freeing the 'vast majority' of roughly $600-650m of annual adjusted free cash flow for repurchases.
WEX.why: The mechanism is three-legged. (1) The buyback is the earnings engine: against a $6.81bn market cap, $600m-plus of FCF routed almost entirely to repurchase is retiring close to a tenth of the float a year, and share count is already down 9.57% year over year to 34.08m. (2) Fuel price and FX flipped from a two-year headwind to a tailwind, while $15m of H2 Mobility pricing actions re-accelerate the largest segment without needing a freight recovery, because management explicitly guided assuming no rebound in miles driven, making any Cass Freight upturn free optionality. (3) The Impactive Capital campaign into the May 2026 annual meeting forced $50m of cost actions and a capital-allocation reset that the market is only now paying for. Valuation is the clincher: 9.76x forward EPS and 6.58x EV/EBITDA against Corpay at 14.13x forward and 12.38x EV/EBITDA. Short interest of 7.61% of shares outstanding, up from 2.19m to 2.59m shares, is adding squeeze fuel into the high.
WEX.risk: Watch: underlying Mobility volumes are still flat and management conceded the trucking improvement is supply-side, not miles driven, so a fuel-price reversal removes both interchange spread and the late-fee income that already cost roughly 2pts of segment growth. Corporate Payments funded volume fell 4% and remains hostage to a handful of OTA contracts, with H2 rate dilution already flagged from travel and embedded mix. WEX Bank's industrial loan charter is the funding backbone, and the $78.4m 2025 credit provision sits on a small-business-heavy fleet book. The average sell-side target of $192.40 is already below spot, so this is a buyback-and-momentum trade rather than a valuation-gap trade: size at two-thirds normal and stop below the 50-day near $167.

The Manhattan Active suite is versionless multi-tenant SaaS sold on five-year-plus contracts; implementation consulting is 47% of revenue and cloud subscriptions 38%, with legacy maintenance in run-off. It serves over 1,200 customers including Walmart, Nike and FedEx, with the top five at only 10% of revenue, and carries no net debt.
MANH.happening: Shares are $213.10, up roughly 79% from the $119.06 52-week low, 26% above the 50-day moving average of $168.64 and 36% above the 200-day at $156.41, with RSI at 71.8. REP.MC.business: Repsol is a Spanish integrated energy company producing about 558 kboe/d of oil and gas, roughly two-thirds gas, refining over 1m barrels per day across six refineries in Spain and Peru, and selling through more than 4,500 service stations, 3,270 of them in Spain, alongside retail electricity, gas and LPG contracts. Segment profit splits roughly 35% upstream, 35% industrial (refining, chemicals, renewable fuels, trading) and 28% customer-facing retail. Fifty-nine percent of sales originate in Spain, making it an Iberian consumer business as much as an oil producer.
REP.MC.happening: The stock is EUR 26.92 after touching a 52-week high of EUR 28.42 on 21 August, up 93.6% over twelve months and 30% above its 200-day moving average of EUR 20.66. The 23 July Q2 report more than doubled adjusted net income to EUR 1.8bn on a refining margin indicator of $14/bbl in the quarter that ran above $30/bbl in July. Repsol answered by raising the second 2026 buyback from EUR 350m to EUR 500m rather than lifting capex, cut net debt EUR 1.1bn to EUR 3.7bn for 11.3% gearing, and delivered Pikka Phase 1 first oil in Alaska with output already running at 580-585 kboe/d by late July.
REP.MC.why: (1) The refining cycle is doing the heavy lifting - tight diesel and jet markets, Strait of Hormuz and Russian supply disruption, and chemicals turning profitable after two years of losses - and management breaks out roughly $2.0-2.2/bbl of the premium as structural biofuels rather than geopolitical, arguing margins hold into 2027. (2) Volume growth is finally real after a 4% production decline in 2025: Pikka ramping toward 80 kbbl/d gross in Q3, Leon-Castile targeted at 19 kbbl/d net by 2027, FY26 guidance moving to the high end of 560-570 kboe/d and 580-600 kboe/d framed for 2026-2028 before any Venezuela upside. (3) Every euro of the windfall is being routed to shareholders rather than the drill bit: EUR 1.051/share of 2026 remuneration, up 8%, a third buyback programme to be announced with Q3 results to hit the 30-40% of CFFO commitment, and share count already down 4.47% year over year. At 6.47x forward earnings, 4.35x EV/EBITDA and a 3.93% yield, Repsol still trades at a clear discount to TotalEnergies at 8.55x forward and 5.24x EV/EBITDA.
REP.MC.risk: Watch: this is a refining-margin trade wearing an integrated-energy costume. The $30/bbl July indicator is not a run-rate, and if Hormuz normalises the 'structural premium' framing is the first thing the market will attack. Venezuela is a live binary - US licences permitting resumption were only re-issued in February 2026 and can be revoked. The Spanish windfall levy and permitting friction concentrate political risk in the home market that generates 59% of sales, and a deliberate EUR 1.3bn working-capital inventory build adds cyclical drag if product prices fall. After a 94% twelve-month run with the average target only EUR 27.63, do not chase the high: build on pullbacks toward the 50-day at EUR 24.51 and stop below it.

BME.L.happening: The shares are 246.8p, 76% above the 140p 52-week low, 16% above the 50-day moving average of 213.64p and 35% above the 200-day at 183.28p - a textbook Stage 2 base breakout off a distress low, though still short of the 269.3p 52-week high. (2) The self-help levers are measurable rather than rhetorical: on-shelf availability of key brands went from 86% at H1 to 93% at H2, revamped December promotions produced +3% UK like-for-likes, and the FMCG SKU rationalisation now rolling across all categories completes in Q3 FY27. BME.L.risk: Watch: UK like-for-likes were still -2.3% in Q1 FY27, and management stated explicitly that FY27 cost mitigation only reaches the bottom line once B&M UK like-for-likes return to growth - which has not happened. SHC.business: Sotera Health is the outsourced sterilization and lab-testing utility for the medical device and pharma industry. Sterigenics runs 48 sterilization plants across 13 countries using ethylene oxide, gamma and X-ray (65% of revenue); Nordion is the world's leading supplier of Cobalt-60, the isotope gamma sterilization consumes (16%); Nelson Labs does the microbiological and analytical testing that validates those processes (19%). Revenue is fee-per-unit-processed under multi-year contracts with more than 2,000 device OEM customers, and over 90% of Sterigenics revenue is contracted.
SHC.happening: The stock gapped 5.2% higher on 6 August on Q2 and has ground to $19.51, within 2% of the $19.85 52-week high and above both the 50-day at $17.86 and the 200-day at $16.68. New CEO Alton Shader's first quarter delivered 8% constant-currency revenue growth and a 51.6% adjusted EBITDA margin, and every FY26 guidance line went up: revenue to $1,236-$1,254m, adjusted EBITDA to $634-$643m, adjusted EPS to $0.95-$1.01, with interest expense cut to $135-$142m after a 100bp repricing on the $1.4bn term loan. Net leverage is 3.0x, inside the 2-3x target, and the former private equity sponsors now hold no stake.
SHC.why: (1) The ethylene oxide litigation overhang that capped this multiple for four years is deflating - the New Mexico claims settled in July for an immaterial amount, leaving Georgia in appeal, and each settlement converts an unquantifiable tail liability into a disclosed number the market can discount. (2) The sponsor overhang is gone and the balance sheet is repaired, leaving a clean compounder on a regulatory lock-in asset: once a facility is written into an FDA submission, moving it requires re-validation and a regulatory filing, which is why Sterigenics has renewed 100% of its top-ten customers for more than five consecutive years. (3) New capacity converts to revenue in H2, with the X-ray facility starting to bill in Q3 as customers finish validation and a large med-tech customer shifting North American EO sterilization from in-house to outsourced. At 12.97x EV/EBITDA and 19.05x forward EPS versus STERIS at 15.00x and 20.63x, the discount to the only comparable global sterilizer has narrowed but not closed, and the $22.72 average target implies 16% upside. Short interest of 14.38m shares, 7.76% of float, is down from 15.84m - covering is part of this move.
SHC.risk: Watch: Nordion's H1 finished above its usual 40-45% of annual revenue on pulled-forward Cobalt-60 harvest shipments, so H2 faces a self-inflicted comparison, and Nelson Labs' 438bp sequential margin jump to 32.4% was explicitly disowned by management as a new base. Georgia EO litigation remains in appeal and is the single item that can re-open the valuation discount overnight. The United States has one commercial supplier of ethylene oxide to the sterilization industry, a genuine single point of failure only partly mitigated by Sotera's own distribution licence, and EPA emissions rules keep tightening capacity at existing sites. Beta is 1.77: keep this at half normal size and stop below the 50-day near $17.85.

Assisted preparation in company-owned and franchised offices is 65% of revenue; the balance is DIY software (10%), international in Canada, Australia, Brazil and India (7%), franchise royalties, Refund Transfers, the Emerald Card and Spruce financial products, and Wave, a small-business accounting and payments platform. The customer base skews lower-to-middle income and refund-anticipating.
HRB.happening: The stock gapped 16.1% on 12 August on 8.4m shares, more than three times the 20-day average, after the 11 August FY26 print: revenue up 4.9% to $3.95bn, adjusted EPS up 13.9%, and an FY27 guide of $4.11-$4.16bn revenue with $6.04-$6.24 adjusted EPS implying roughly 15.6% growth. It touched a 52-week high of $58.67 intraday, sold off 7% to $50.13 on 17 August and has rebuilt to $53.19 - 23% above the 50-day moving average of $43.12 and 38% above the 200-day at $38.53. The quarterly dividend was raised 10% to $0.46.
HRB.why: (1) This is the unwind of the 'AI kills tax prep' de-rating that dragged the stock to a $28.16 low, and the rebuttal was operational rather than rhetorical: conversion up 200bps, which CEO Curtis Campbell called the largest single-year improvement in company history, retention up 190bps, US assisted volume up 2% and net average charge up 4.1% on 3pts of price and 1pt of mix. (2) The EPS algorithm is price plus buyback rather than volume - roughly $400m of repurchase planned in FY27 against a $6.56bn market cap, share count already down 6.17% year over year, and $756m of FY26 free cash flow against a $53 share price. (3) The short base is the accelerant: 17.32m shares, 14.05% of shares outstanding and 9.23 days to cover, down from 19.12m the prior month and still the most crowded short in this cohort. At 8.65x forward EPS, 7.47x EV/EBITDA and an 11.5% free cash flow yield with a 3.46% dividend, HRB trades near half Intuit's 14.08x EV/EBITDA.
HRB.risk: Watch: management conceded industry filing growth will moderate below the typical 1% as job growth cools, and said holding assisted share only underpins the low end of the FY27 guide - the midpoint and high end require outperformance. The FY27 effective tax rate steps up from 14% to about 23%, so reported comparisons get structurally harder. DIY revenue grew 0.2%, franchise royalties fell 3.9% and financial services revenue is shrinking, so the growth is narrow. All profit is earned between January and April, so a single disrupted filing season is unrecoverable. With the average target at $50.67, below spot, and the 17 August 7% single-day reversal showing how fast a 14%-short name unwinds both ways, take partial profits into strength and stop below the gap fill near $46.
